div.head: POULTRY PEN.
div.p: POULTRY PEN.
HINTS AND INTERESTING FACTS AND CHATS FOR AMATEURS.
COMING EGG FAMINE.

It is more than doubtful whether the great] majority of people have any accurate under- standing of the real state of affairs in the egg industry, and it is, time that the facts were fairly stated and the situation faced. It is, of course, realised by most people that eggs are dear, but how many have any concep- tion of what the position is likely to be as re- gards-the searcity during the-rapidly- approach- ing autumn and winter? • , How are consumers' wants supplied? Where do the eggs come from? • , The broad answer is that in normal times we import eggs to the value of £10,000,000, out of our total consumption of about ,R 24,000,000 worth—wholesale value. At any rate it is a matter of fact that before the war we were paying about £26,000 or more daily for eggs imported from foreign countries. These im- ported eggs were sent to us from Russia, Den- mark, Germany, France, Italy, Austria, Hol- land, the Balkans, Morocco, Egypt, &c.
Look to the Future!

The Board of Agriculture bids us "Look to the future." That is sound, common sense advice, and it should be accepted by poultry- keepers of all descriptions. In addition to emergency efforts to cope with the more immediate situation, it is imperative to look further ahead and prepare for the future. If we will, we can increase our output up to a value of £30,000,000 without interfering with any other stock or crop on our land—and this on agricultural holdings alone. It would only mean that our farmers and small-holders should increase their stock up to an average of three fowls per acre. But that by no means covers the possibilities, because it takes no account of poultry-keepers on areas of less than one acre. The opportuni- ties for cottagers and the occupants of subur- ban gardens and town backyards are enormous. They should be able to supply their own needs, and in many cases have surplus eggs for sale. If we will, we can in the future not only capture but hold our own markets, but to do so we must preserve all useful breeding and lay- ing stock. This is the hour of opportunity and prepara- tion, as well as the hour of trial.—" The Poultry World."

div.head: RISING PRICES.
div.p: RISING PRICES.

It has been prophesied that during the com- ing winter eggs will be in demand at 3d. each says "The Feathered World." And there is reason in the prediction, because of the un- usual shortage of laying stock in the country. People are just now beginning to realise that there is likely to be a dearth of egg supplies shortly, and those with accommodation for keeping stock are briskly looking around at the moment for specimens which are likely to meet the prospective emergency. I never knew a stronger demand, and prices are exceptionally tempting._ .

Those who have been accustomed to procuring their stock of laying fowls for the purpose of supplying household requirements at from 3s. ed. to ss. per head will be more or less sur- prised, in this year of difficulties, when they are asked from 7s. 6d. to 10s. per head for pure- bred breeds of reliable character.

But it must be calculated that, whilst the cost of rearing following high cost of feeding has been alarmingly heavy this year, has in itself increased the individual value of each bird, the few 1915 bred birds there are available adds to their price, the lack of supplies having an automatic influence in this direction with all commodities. It must be considered, how- ever, that if eggs are going to be anything like the. price we have mentioned, a reliably-bred layer will quickly pay for her cost, even if it reaches 10s.

div.head: NATIONAL EGG COLLECTION FOR THE WOUNDED.
div.p: THE NATIONAL EGG COLLECTION FOR THE WOUNDED.

The Secretary of the Executive Committee, Mr. F. Carl (" Poultry World "), writes :—" We have been issuing broadcast urgent appeals for new-laid eggs to go to our wounded soldiers and sailors ia hospital, and we have been successful in collecting several millions of eggs for this valuable purpose. Our supplies have, unfor- tunately, during the past fortnight, shown serious signs of diminution, owing no doubt to the time of the year and the fact that hens are not laying quite so well, and we should be very grateful, therefore, if contributors could either send us a further small supply of eggs or a small sum in cash to enable us to purchase the supplies we need. With the growth of military operations the demand for new-laid eggs on the part of our wounded is unfortunately increas- ing to over 500,000 per week."

div.head: FARMERS' PROFITS.
div.p: FARMERS' PROFITS.
Is The Government Entitled To Share In Them?
The agricultural problem must be looked straight in the face, said the Marquis of Lin- colnshire, at a farmers' meeting at Bucking- ham on Saturday. _ . .

Prices had gone up, and tenant farmers were doing well, very well. If times were, normal at present prices it would be only just and fair —as rents were reduced some years ago by 20, 30 and even 35 per cent.—that in this rising prosperity the landlords should have a share. But we were at war, and if any English land- lord should take advantage of the great rise in prices, and think there should be a general rise in rents, it would receive, and deserve, stern condemnation.

Nevertheless, the tenant farmers could not properly, claim the whole advantage. No Government would be able to fix a minimum or maximum price either for wheat or meat, but agriculturists must recognise the fact that if food prices should rise to an ab- normal extent which God forbid farmers must not expect the whole profits to go into their pockets but; like manufacturers, must expect a. limitation of war. profits. Land- lords and tenants must recognise the possibility. cif this being necessary.
MiIMOIN

The Mayor then announced that he had re- ceived a number of letters of apology regret- ting. inability to attend, including the following from Mr. John J. Bleckly : "I am whole- heartedly iii favour of inaugurating a practical movement for the purpose of stimulating and encouraging both public and personal economy, with the object of counteracting; as far as pos- sible, the enormous financial drain upon the resources of the country, arising from the war, and I am convinced that, unless an earnest and effectual effort is made _forthwith in this direc- tion, something 'very :nearly approaching national bankruptcy will shortly have to be faced, should the war continue, as it seems probable that it will,, for another year or two. It is our duty, one and all, to put an end to what it is no exaggeration to describe as the wicked Parliamentary, municipal and personal extravagance that the.country has of late years drifted into, under the mischievous political and social guidance and example of 'many of its leaders in all ranks .of society, high and low, and which has done much to sap the founda- tions of natiQnal prosperity and to lower the tone of political and private life. Whilst Germany Saved - •

"While our enemies in Germany have been carefully husbanding and economising all their resources, we, in this country, have been lav- ishly squandering ours, and unless we promptly put our house in order in this respect, they will outlast us in the present death struggle— which they have forced upon us—with conse- quences to the British Empire and the whole civilised world of inconceivable disaster."

After reading this letter his Worship added: "So far as the Town Council or Warrington is concerned, I can say that we have stopped spending any money, unless it is absolutely necessary for the immediate welfare of the people of the tqwn." (Hear, hear.)

THE IMPORTANCE OF THE QUESTION. Mr. C. E. Parker detailed the circumstances under which he and Mr. Rylands were prompted to approach the Mayor with a view to his Worship launching the thrift scheme locally. He went on to add that something in a similar direction had been done locally before any national scheme was inaugurated. . A number of those who were interested in the Guild of Help felt some time ago that the matter was so important that they decided that they would act on their own account, and accordingly called a committee together and framed circulars, and so on, which were intended for the guidance of the people. Later came the inauguration of the present national movement, and, of course, it went without saying that so vast a question should be dealt with nationally. Hence meet- ings like that one in the various towns and dis- tricts up and down the country !• He did not think it was really necessary \ to press the importance of this question on the people as a whole; they had already begun to realise it! The point had been before the public so much, and the presence there that night of so repre- sentative a gathering proved that the ladies and gentlemen of Warrington, in various walks of life, were realising to the full the importance of the question. The Problem of the " Fixed Wealth."

He thought that, perhaps naturally, the. im- portance of the military situation had, lately„ somewhat obscured from their minds the ques- tion of the financial aspect of the war, import- ant as they all realised that to be. It was a curious thing, when we came to weigh it up, that whilst this was undoubtedly the richest country in the world, a country possessing un- told wealth—wealth which, if it could be realised, would keep the war going for a very long time—that wealth was of such a character that only a small proportion of it was avail- able. In other words, that wealth was, 60 to speak, largely fixed wealth; they could not transplant, for instance, from South America, or their colonies, all their vast interests—inter- ests that were world-wide. The result was that they were thrown back upon that portion of the national wealth which they might describe as wealth of a liquid character; and it was only upon such wealth that ,they could depend. He thought, perhaps, the people were a little apt to be misled by the ease with which the country raised the huge sum of £600,000,000 for the War Loan. •
Nearly All " Liquid " Capital at Present Absorbed.

They had to remember. that that loan had ab- sorbed, if not all, at any rate practically all, of the available liquid capital of the country. The difficulty would arise when they had to repeat that gigantic money-raising process—repeat it, perhaps, not only once, but even twice. Thus it would mean that they would have, • as a nation, to fall back not upon what they had already saved, but upon what they could save—rich and poor alike, for on both sections of the commu- nity did it now depend, in greater or lesser de- gree, as to whether the country would be able to stand the enormous financial strain that the war had brought about. Of course, the posi- tion in other countries was very much the same as in their own, and the question was one that would assume even far greater importance as the months went by. Germany realised the difficulty far sooner than this country did. It had been stated in the papers that Germany's scheme of regulating the bread supply had en- abled them to cut down the consumption of that very necessary comestible by at least one-half. Whether that was 'wise or not, was -another question, hat, undoubtedly, they would have

The internal expenditure of the State was not a matter of so very great importance, but what was of vital importance were the purchases which they, as a nation, made from 'abroad. It was perfectly Clear that when a nation was liv- ing on its capital and at the same time was buy- ing things from abroad that it could do without, it was liquidating so much of its capital as was represented by the value of the imported goods which it purchased. It was of vital importance that the people of this country should recognise the economic side of the issue and that, so far as possible, they should save every penny that they possibly could. Despite the strain of war, the conditions of trade in this country were good—wages were good and there were plenty of oppOrtudities for saving! He had heard of cases in Lancashire—particularly in Wigan— where something like £lO or ..tl4 a week was going into the houses of workers. The rate of unemployment was never lower than it was at .the present moment; and there was, generally, a very grave risk that the working classes—en- joying specially great prosperity in view of the wages that they are earning—might be tempted to live extravagantly; That would have two effects; the first being that they were losing the opportunity of putting by for "the rainy day," which was, undoubtedly, before them, and the second that they would find themselves handi- capped severely when those times of grave de- pression—which he thought extremely likely— came along after the .war was over. Trade Depression When War Ends.

He was sorely afraid that, following the con- clusion of peace, there would be great trade depression, for the time being, all over the world, and the workers might find themselves face to face with a very poor reward indeed for their labour, besides being faced with the pro- blem of a very large percentage of unemployed. That fact must be impressed on the minds of all. It was the ambition of every person in France to own some Government stock; the French people liked to feel that they had got a little income from Government securities. It would be a splendid thing to inculcate the same desire into the minds of the British people. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Saving for "Rainy hay" Urged at Town's Meeting.
div.p: Saving for "Rainy hay" Urged at Town's Meeting.
LOCAL COMMITTEE APPOINTED.

This meeting considers the question of thrift to be of vital importance to the country at the present time, both for the successful prosecu- tion of the war and for meeting the situation after the war. It therefore urges the inaugura- tion of a local educational campaign in favour of economy, and to this end appoints a com- mittee to consist of 20 persons, at least six of whom shall be ladies, with power to co-opt.

The foregoing resolution was passed at a well- attended and representative town's meeting, held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) on Monday evening. Those present 'included representatives of practically every phase of local public life.

to realise, far more than their people had hitherto done, that they would, rich and poor alike, have to cut down their expenditure, whilst the lesson would specially have to be borne home upon all spending corporations, who would have to cut down their expenses very seriously. "Living in an Extravagant Manner."

The term " extravagance " was somewhat relative. Whilst the country was going o.i well, and individuals were doing well, what could now be called extravagance could not then, fairly, have been called extravagance. But at the present time, when there was such need to huisband the resources of the' nation, there could be no doubt but that, as a whole they were living in an extravagant manner. Here was a species of war service which all of them could render. Age and infirmities prevented many of them flora taking an active part in the military duties devolvinl on the nation, but old and young, men and wonoin, could take a part in this thrift can)paign. Thc4e of them who were climbing up Hill 60 or eve % Hill 70—(laugh- ter and applause)—were in this matter of national thrift given an opportunity of doing a share. Mr. Parker concludA by proposing the resolution quoted above.
DIFFICULT ECONOMICAL PROPOSITION.

Mr. W. Peter Eylands seconded, and in doing so said that he was afraid it must be admitted- that on the whole the British were not naturally a thrifty nation. It was a very difficult thing to get a whole race to change their habits unless the necessity could be brought home to their minds with dominating force. Individual and national thrift were of greater ipaportance.now than at any other time, though they were always important. ‘Hear, hear National thrift was a ' somewhat difficult economical proposition, and it was by no means easy to put the case for it in a plain and suc- cinct manner. A country could carry on ear for an extraordinarily long time by hypothecat- ing all it had got, but the pressure came when the time arrived for the clearing Up ot the financial men and when it was found that the country could no longer live on its capital. The inevitable day of reckoning was bound to come, and the penalty had got to be paid. When an individual was faced with some critical period— when he was hit in some heavy capital manner and was face to face with heavy expenses—he at once curtailed his expenditure; he indulged in a compulsory form of thrift. The same was axiomatic of the State, for that was composed of the individuals. At the present time the State was faced with enormous expenditure, the great bulk of which was raised out of capital, and it was only by making the people realise that the capital which the State was expending was their own capital that they were going to g.t the people to be thrifty. div.head: WHY THE MEETING WAS CALLED.
div.p: WHY THE MEETING WAS CALLED.

In opening the meeting the Mayor said that they must all have read in the papers about the necessity for exercising thrift. He had re- ceived a requisition asking him to call that meeting, the requisition being signed by Mr. C. E. Parker on behalf of the local Liberal Associa- tion, and by Mr. W. Peter Rylands on behalf of the Conservative Association. In the requisi- tion those gentlemen, pointed out that their re- spective Associatious. had been requested by the Government to use their organisations with a view to instilling the need for more thrift- into the minds of the people of Warrington. Both the kefitlemen named thought the best means of attaining the desired end would be for ,the civic head of the borough to call .a meeting with a view to appointing a committee to further the object in hand. They all knew that the country was Aassing through a very serious crisis, and that One Of the most important things they had to consider was how they might husband their resources so as to provide for what:Might be_a very long struggle. There was more than a touch of the times • in which we live—the nerve-harassing day is of a war which may yet become world-wide—about the assemblage on Speech Day, which, this year, was Wednesday this week—at the Boteler Gram- mar School, for not only did each of the three speakers dilate upon the war and the duties, burdens and responsibilities which it entails for all, but nearly all the seats along one side of the assembly-hall were occupied by smart khaki-clad figures of several sizes—the members of the newly-formed school Cadet Corps; every one of them a more or less miniature replica of the gallant lads of the 4th South Lancs., now resting within earshot of the booming guns of friend and 'foe, after having covered themselves. with glory in fierce hand-to-hand fighting. Speech Day proceedings—much curtailed this year—opened with an inspection of the Cadets, who were drawn up in two soldierly-looking lines on the playing field at the •rear of, the old school, and who, to the admiration of a small company of members of the governing body of I the school and a few privileged guests, went smartly through a few military evolutions. The inspection over, came an adjournment to the assembly room of the school, where the I prizes were distributed by the Rector of War- rington (the Rev. Canon F. W. Willis), who pre- sided over the proceedings, and who was sup- 'ported by, the, following members of 'the Board of Governors: 'Alderman. A. Bennett, Alderman. Smethurst, Councillor IL Roberts,. (who is also chairman of the Warrington • Education Cona- mittee), Mr. W. Peter Rylands, Mr. R. Forshaw and Mr. Vere B. Davies (the clerk to the Governors).

had attended ,the 'inauguration of the Cadet Corps. (Applause.) The smart, military 'ap- pearance of all the boys wearing the uniform was a source of satisfaction and of pride to the governors. (Applause.) In a time like the pre- sent, when the nation was passing through a very critical time—a time when the people were consumed with daily anxieties—it was right that all of them, young and old, should be doing something that brought the war home to their minds. The older ones among that gathering, in their daily affairs, were nearly all engaged in war service of one kind or another, and it was but becoming that they, the rising hope of the nation, should don the uniform and undergo drill, so that they might feel that they, in some small way, were playing their, part, even if that part only consisted in showing those who were old enough to do the fighting that there were others coming along behind who were prepared to take theileplaces in the years to come, should the need arise. div.p: QUESTION OF MOVING THE SCHOOL.

Councillor Roberts was the next, and last, speaker. The other day, he said, he was read- ing a letter written by a schoolmistress in Australia, and which was published in most of the papers. The letter was addressed to the Australian "boys" who had gone out to the Dardanelles and had done so much to make history. The letter was full of pathos and of the highest and most idealistic sentiment and, for a true definition of what duty was, a better letter he had never seea; it ought to be circu- lated throughout the length and breadth of the country. It appealed particularly to the lads of Australia, but in sentiment and purpose it was just as applicable to the lads in that room as it also was to any other of the inhabitants of the great British Empire. Councillor Roberts went on to say that he had been very glad to learn of the formation of the Cadet Corps in connec- tion with the school. For several years he had been a convert to the principle of National Ser- vice. He had not hesitated, at considerable risk of misunderstanding, to express himself on every suitable occasion, clearly and definitely on that point. For the life of him, he could not understand why, when the people were com- pelled to do so many things that were of com- paratively slight importance, the one thing which the present circumstances had proved to be more important than anything else—the pre- paration and the training of the individual to take his fair part in the defence of the country —should have been left purely to voluntary effort.

But, if he could not join himself, he had made up for it by contributing two sons. {Cheers). From old scholars of the school had gone forth a fine body of men to serve King and country; to play their part in the greatest war of righteousness the world had even seen, and to bring credit to the old school to which they were so proud to have belonged. (Cheers.) One of them had given his life—his all—and they must remember his name in gratitude and reverent respect. He (the speaker) hoped that every boy in the school, as time wont on am as he grew older and more capable of bearing the burden, which every citizen would have to bear, would feel it not simply a duty but a pleasure to maintain the traditions of the school, and to extend them and increase them and make the name of the school one that would be remembered with gratitude for many years to come. Whilst the burden of the war fell very heavily on the younger men of to-day, the older men felt the burden, the sadness and the utter wickedness of the whole terrible business, perhaps, to a greater degree than the younger men.
When the War is Over

When the war was over and this country, with her Allies, had attained success—that suc- cess which was necessary for the future peace and the civilisation of the whole world—thete would be burdens laid on the shoulders of the future generation greater tlup had fallen on the shoulders of the people for many generations, and he wanted the lads whom he was addressing to feel that whatever position they might have to occupy in the days to come, wherever they might be placed in the great British Empire, the first and the last thing they should,remem- ber was to try and ascertain their duty to the State to which they belonged, and to the locality in which they happened to live, and to do their very best to carry out that duty honourably, conscientiously and to the best of their ability. (Hear, hear.) He had no fear for the future, knowing, as he 'did, the calibre of the youth of the country. The picture before him of bright, fine, intelligent, able and clever boys—more than all, English boys; like unto whom there were no other lads in the world—inspired him with confidence for the future of the country. Great as it had been in the past, the country would be greater still in the future; it would be better served by the coming generation than it had been by those who would soon, in the inexorable course of time, soon have to lay down the charge committed to them. (Applause.) The assembled company then joined in sing- ing the first verse of the National Anthem, and the proceedings of a memorable Speech Day were at a close.

Although a cycle is a mechanical affair, yet there is life in it. It is an extremely difficult thing to state in words exactly what this term means, but any experienced rider can tell the *instant he mounts a machine whether it re- sponds ,to him. A live cycle will give back in its running every ounce of energy which the rider exerts. A dead machine will require con- siderably more energy to propel it. The ques- tion of life is really one of design and construc- tion. The frame must be rigid, the alignment of the chain wheels perfect, the,. wheels true with the spokes at the right tension, and the bearings must be well constructed. Some well- known firms are so particular that they pass all the balls for the bearings through a special machine, which will throw out those that are not perfectly round, and those which, being round, vary 1/10,000 inch. It is only in this way that life can be secured in a mount.

div.head: CLERGY WIDOWS AND DAUGHTERS.
div.p: CLERGY WIDOWS AND DAUGHTERS.
A Successful Year And Bright Prospects.
DARLEY DALE MEETING.

The annual meeting or the subscribers to the Clergy Widows' and Orphans' Fund, which, founded in 1697, has provided grants for the widows and education for the orphans of the clergy of the Chester, Liverpool and Manchester diocese, was held at Darley Dale, Derbyshire, on Tuesday.. St. Elphin's Clergy Daughters' School was founded at Warrington in 1844, but new buildings were bought at Darley Dale in 1904, and the local buildings were absorbed by the Training College. . The Lord Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) occupied the chair, and those present included the Rev. G. B. Thurston, reetor of Lymm (honorary secretary of the widows' and orphans' fund); the Rev. Canon Willis,- rector of War- rington, and rural dean of Winwick (honorary secretary of the school); the Rev. Ti. V. Pigot (rector of Grappenhall), the Rev. W. T. War- burton (Chester), and Mr. George H. Smith (representing Mr. Henry Greenall, the honorary treasurer). INCREASED SUCCESS OF THE SCHOOL. The Rev. Canon Willis, in his report on the school, said they had had another satisfactory year, the number of scholars being above the average. Except for a slight epidemic of Ger- man measles of a mild type, the health of the pupils had been excellent. The standard of the staff had been 'maintained. The new science room and the new cookery rooms had been much appreciated and fully utilised, and the school had generally benefited by the generous gift which had been -made through the Bishop of Chester. The recently-established' ' Kennedy Bursaries had been in use this year, and were doing good work. _ _

The Continued increase in the number of pupils [now 1151, whilst extremely satisfactory, was taxing the school accommodation to the utmost, and if the increase was maintained, and, perhaps, surpassed, it would be difficult to find adequate accommodation. If the war did not interfere with the development of the school and did not cause the numbers to fall, it would probably be necessary for the committee in the near future to consider the advisability of open- ing a junior preparatory house. The alternative arrangement would be to have a hostel for the staff. The committee wished to record their continued confidence in the head mistress and her staff, and their appreciation of the, excellent and thorough work done at the school. (Ap- plause.) _ _ _
FLOURISHING FINANCES.
Increased Grants to Widows and Orphans.

The Hon. Trea urer s report stated' that the 4 - income for the year 1914 again showed a satis- factory increase of over .1300, due to additional receipts for school fees, and the full operatioft of the finance schemes of the Chester and Man- chester Diocesan Finance Association, and an increase in the grant from the Lord Bishop of Liverpool's Fund. The expenditure had un- avoidably been heavier, but at the end of the year there was a small balance in the bank.

The Rev. G. B. Thurston. reported that the committee having considered the question of grants to widows and orphans, recommended the following amounts be submitted to the sub- scribers: Chester..; diocese, 24 widows and 20 orphans, .745; Liverpool diocese, 17 widows and 17 orphans. ,t 520 Manchester diocese, 40 widows and 14 orphans, £855; six parents' scholarships? £270; making a total. of £2,390, or an increase of £195 on the previous year. The committee,. owing to increased income, were able to increase the number and amounts of grants to Widows and orphans. The year closed with a credit balance at the bankers of £315 2s. 7d., which would enable the committee to deal with further necessitous cases. A legacy of £43 is., one-half of the residue of her estate, had been left to the society by the late Miss C. E. Marlin, of 5, Rawson-road, Seaforth. The following were appointed representatives on the three Diocesan Finance Committees: Chester, the Rev. G. B. Thurston and Mr. John Coxon; Manchester, the Bishon of Whalley and Mr. W. P. Fullagar; Liverpool, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn and Mr. H. S. Woodcock. The reports were adopted.

div.p: ST. ELPHIN'S SCHOOL.
Prize Money Diverted For War
Comforts.
The annual prize giving took place in the school in the presence of a large number of parents, pupils and visitors, the Lord Bishop again presiding,. _ _ -

The Head Mistress. Miss Flood, said that the committee were of the 'opinion—and she shared that opinion—that, as the country was passing through a time of great anxiety, there should be a curtailment of the usual prize-giving cere- mony. The entertainment usually nrovided would also be omitted. The girls had volun- tarily resigned their prizes, and would receive certificates instead. The committee of the school and the donors of the prizes had kindly allowed them to use the money usually contributed for the purchase of nrizes for the purchase of material for knitting and sewing during the winter months to provide comrorts for our sol- diers and sailors. (Applause.)

div.head: BISHOP ON SELF-SACRIFICE AND SELF-DISCIPLINE.
div.p: BISHOP ON SELF-SACRIFICE AND SELF-DISCIPLINE.

The Bishop said he was sure they would all agree that the Head Mistress was perfectly right in the course she had adopted, and they must thank the pupils of the school for the spirit of self-sacrifice they had displayed in giving up their prizes in order that they might provide funds to make garments of various kinds for Our soldiers and sailors. (Applause.) The ques- tion was being asked, "What can we do to help our country in a time like this?" What could the girls of that school do for their country's good at the Present critical moment? There were three things they could do, and he •would tell them what they were in three words—ser- vice, self-sacrifice, prayer. (Hear, hear.) One great characteristic of the school was that it turned out pure, modest girls, certainly full of life, as they wished them to be, but likely, when they grew up to women,, to be a glory to woman- hood. The girls of the school could serve the country by carrying, into their daily lives the lessons of purity, modesty and devotion they • had learnt from their teachers. a

One great lesson God is teaching England to- day, continued the Bishop, is sell-discipline. Years and years ago M. Gladstone said that English men and English women needed self- discipline. Germany owed a great deal. of .its greatness to its self-discipline. Its .people, had been disciplined and taught to obey, and the girls of that school could render no higher ser- vice to their country than by being well disci- plined and teaching self-discipline to others. (Applause.) They could also serve theizscoun- try by such self-sacrifice, as that shown, by their willingneis to give up receiving the usual prikee. Certainly our soldier's At the Front were teach- ing us what, we had scarcely realised. before-- the. beauty of self-sacrifice: .•(Applause.). We could all show a spirit of self-sacrifice bYAiving on. a simpler and plainer fare than we had done in the past, and thus exercise economy. • (Ap- plause.) _ _ _ _

Mrs. Allan Bright, Liverpool (president for the year), who distributed the certificates to the pupils, was cordially thanked, on the motion of the Rev. Canon Willis, seconded by the Rev. G. B. Thurston.

The Bishop, replying to a vote of thanks for occupying the chair, said he had been trying for fifteen long years to abolish votes of thanks in the diocese of Liverpool. Tie confessed that he had completely failed. (Laughter.)

div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.
CHAT and GOSSIP.
• By MARJORIE.
The Court Circular.

The official records of the daily movements of crowned heads differ considerably in the various Courts of Europe. In Russia, for instance, the Court Circular is regarded as a very important ,announcement, and is a much older institution than is the case in this country. Our own Court Circular, which, it was said a short time ago, was going to be discontinued, is very modern in comparison, for it dates only from the early days of Queen Victoria's married life. It was deemed advisable then to issue a daily record of the doings of the Royal Family on account of the scurrilous attacks on the Prince Consort made by even leading newspapers. The most misleading statements appeared also in connection with other Royal personages, and with regard to the daily life of the Court, which it was hoped the official announcement would disprove and counteract. Thrift and Food Reform.

Rich and poor, old and young, all are invited to join the great army of economisers. Thrift, as it is practised on the Continent, is better understood in Scotland than in England, but the London County Council proposes to catch the economist young, and it has instructed head masters and mistresses in all its schools to en- courage saving among the children. In France the boy saves for his career, the girl for her dot, and the housewife invariably has her own long stocking. To the same end, the Government has issued a penny cookery book, entitled "Economy in food," which says at the outset, for the benefit of the cook and Mary Jane, as well as for the housewife, that we must save money, eat less meat, and be careful about food. It gives a number of recipes for simple dinners, and cheap dishes, and also many use- ful cookery hints. It is the middle, class house- wife, with time to spare to prepare meat-substi- tute dishes, who can do most in the reform of her scheme of cooking and home management. A good method for testing an oven to ascer- tain if it is hot enough for baking purposes is as follows :—Place a piece of white paper on the shelf of the oven and leave it for five minutes. Spoiling Good Peas. When peas are coming in so plentifully we must try and not let the cook spoil them with any fancy notions of foreign cooks. Among the recipes one sees in cookery books for the im- provement of peas we find pepper, sugar, mint, milk, seasoning, parsley, flour, carrots, stock, eggs, and so o.n, all unnecessary, the peas being far better simply boiled. Such additions might be useful in the case of hard peas of the Conti- nental garden, but never for ours. The use of mint, too, is offensive to many, and its use will not make bad peas eatable. div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular . Language.
Treatment of Burns.

A physician writes :—Free use of soft soap upon a fresh burn will remove the fire from the flesh in less time than it takes to write these words. If the burn be severe, after relief from the pain use linseed oil, and then sift upon it wheat flour. When this is dried hard, repeat the oil and flour until . a complete covering is obtained. Let this dry until it falls off, and a new skin will be formed without a scar. This treatment leaves nothing more to be desired. Strong Babies.

The myth of the infant Hercules who strangled two serpents in his cradle may not have been a myth at all, but a fact, a Paris correspondent writes to the "London Tele- graph." Modern science has proved that it is quite a possible feat. The new-born babe is relatively much stronger than a full-grown man, according to the results of medical tests. "The muscles of the, forearm are surprisingly vigorous. A few hours after birth a baby sus- pended by its finger to a stick, or to the finger of a person, can hold itself in the air for 10 seconds, and, in the case of particularly strong infants; for as long as half a minute. At four days old the child's strength has increased, and the time is two and a half minutes for 98 per cent of babies. The maximum is attained at a fortnight. Few infants can hang on for more than one and a half minutes, though one exceptional young Hercules remained sus- pended for two minutes and thirty-eight seconds by his right hand. After that he still hung on with his left for 15 seconds longer." Foods That Give Bulk.

All vegetable foods contain more or less cellulose, but the amount differs very greatly. This element, as has already' been mentioned, is highly necessary as a means of securing normal bowel action. Indeed, bulk, not simply in the food itself, but in the residues left be- hind after the absorption of the nutritive por- tions of the food, is of first importance. This quality in food is even more important than the antiseptic properties, for the -reason that putrefactive bacteria may always find in the bile and other irktestinal secretions abundant material to support their growth, provided sufficient delay occurs to encourage putrefactive changes. The thing most necessary in the pre- vention of putrefaction is rapidity of movement of food residues and body waste along the in- testine to the exit. Fine flour bread should be wholly discarded from the bill of fare, giving way to bread or biscuit made from whole-wheat meal or rye flour. Wheat meal and bran pre- pared from thoroughly washed wheat should be used, for both contain enormous quantities of dirt and bacteria, which are especially harmful to persons suffering from constipation.—Dr. Kellogg.

Arthur Hepworth, of no fixed abode, was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, before Mr. S. Wright (in the chair), Aldermen Pierpoint, Salton, Smethurst and Jas. Evans, and Messrs. W. Furness and G. Pilling, with stealing two pint glasses, the pro- perty of Messrs. The Chief Constable, in applying for a re- mand in Order that the police might make in- quiries into prisoner's antecedents„ stated that at six o'clock on Saturday evening prisoner was in the lodging-house kept by Mr. G/eeson, Town Hill, when he took from his pocket a large glass (produced) and irent to a fellow lodger and asked him if. he would purchase it. Prisoner took another out of his pocket and put it on the mantelpiece.
"I'm Telling the Police of This."

The deputy looked at it, and finding it bore the initials of Messrs. Walker's firm, he said to prisoner: "I'm telling the police of this." Sergeant Kenwright was told, and inquiries were made, as a result of which it was found out that prisoner went into the Lower Angel under the influence of drink. The people of the house re- fused to serve him. He then asked for some cigarettes. - Asked if he had anything to say, prisoner said, "I was drunk at the time." The Chief Constable: Whether he was drunk or not, he said to the policeman who asked him where he got the glasses: "Mind your own - business."
The adjournment was granted. The Adjourned Appearance.

He came over when the war broke out with the intention of joining the Army. He had tried several times to join, but they v ould not have him on account of his eyesight. Re- cently he tried to join the Naval Reserve, and the authorities had replied (letter produced and handed to the magistrates). div.head: NEW POTATOES.
div.p: NEW POTATOES.
Advice That Might Have Undesired Consequences.

If we are not careful our efforts to conserve food supplies, and to encourage economy in their use, may imperil methods of production which have beet' developed as the result of practice and science operating in prudent harmony. _ _

The Board of Agriculture have appealed to the public to refrain from buying new potatoes until the old crop has been exhausted. The advice is sound in so far as the individual householder is concerned, since new potatoes are more or less a luxury and their use implies a measure of extravagance. A wider or national survey, however, reveals serious objections to the recommendation. The new potatoes obtain- able in the summer months are grown under conditions that make them expensive to the consumer, but a substantial gain to the nation. They are virtually a catch crop of exceptional value. Their production is part of a system that gives to the nation two crops in the year instead of one. They are harvested any time from early in June till the middle of July, and as soon as it is cleared the land is tilled and sown or planted with another crop. To leave the new potatoes to mature might add from one to two tons of tubers per acre, but this would be obtained at the expense of a full crop of cabbages or other vegetables, ryegrass or vetches, all equally valuable in their respective localities as food for man or animal. This year especially we shall need all the catch crops we can raise.

Intensive farming in crop or stock produc- tion increases the returns from the land, but it involves risks and expenditure that are' warranted only by the higher prices obtained for the produce. The readiness of the wealthier classes to pay for the luxury of commodities out of season conduces indirectly to ampler seasonable supplies at moderate prices.—" The Times."

div.head: YEAR OF WAR,
div.p: A YEAR OF WAR,

A year ago this week-end this country was holidaying with an uneasy feeling that tronble was brewing for a great part of Europe,: but we hoped that we should not be drawn into the seething mass of destruction. It was just twelve months last Wednes- day, since Austria so unjustifiably drew the sword against Servia, and, so quickly did events move, that it will be twelve months next Wednesday since we accepted the inso- lent challenge of Germany when that country had decided to trample on the rights of Bel- gium ia order to hack a way through to Paris. Commenting on the event in the first few days of the War, "The Examiner " laid the blame at the door of the GERMAN EMPEROR, and said that this nation. had no quarrel with the Ger- man people. We wish we could still say the same thing: Time has- shown that the Ger- man people have been very apt pupils of their misguided and hypocritical ruler, who has sent- ' millions of his fellows to an untimely grave and proclaimed the while that he is the special instrument of the ALMIGHTY.' 'There may be traces of sanity in Germany, but sanity has not proclaimed itself in very practical form so far. These self-same people that we were willing, even after the outbreak of war, to credit with higher aims in this Twentieth 'Cen- tury than the cutting of human throats, have not .scrupled at anything to carry into effect the wishes of their gentle overlord. They have -sunk helpless and innocent travellers at sea, they have manufactured poisonous gasses to tortdre brave adversaries on land; • they have bombarded watering-places, they have mal- treated prisoners, and they have oppressed Poland, .France and Belgium beyond all description. They have done such things as

have justified Loan DEBBY in saying that the ambition of an Englishman should be. before he dies to kill a German. The fact is that we have got past all the arguing or considering stages. The German will do .all that can be done, however devilish, to help to achieve his object; and all we need concern ourselves

about is not to argue with him or dispute among ourselves, but to do all we can to en- compass his destruction. All things considered, we think there are grounds for congratulation. At the time of writing there are fears that Warsaw may fall, but originally Russia did not intend to defend Warsaw, and the twelve months that have been needed by Germany to take the place has cod our adversaries hundreds of thousands ot men, and, above all, more time than they thought they could safely spare upon the whole campiagn. If the Russian Army re- mains intact, our great Ally will still be able

to givi Germany as much as Germany can manage in the East. On the West we and France ere stronger than ever, and full of cottftdenee as to the result. when the testing time comes. Paris lies as far removed from -the enemy as it did two months after the war began. As to the accession of allies the ad- vantage undoubtedly rests with us, for, while am unspeakable Turk has, quite naturally, joined the polluters of Belgium, Italy has joined the battle on the side of freedom, and other liberal' and enlightened r nations may

very soon follow. Besides, Germany has estranged neutral countries by sinking their ships and shedding the blood of their citizens, thus setting up, as in the case of the United Stites, a very dangerous feeling of antagonism and hate that may easily burst out into flame. We are suffering severely in many ways, but we have the measure of our enemy, and may look forward with confidence, providing we all pull together, to the final extermination of Prussianism. The peoples of the ci;irised world will then be able to breathe more freely and follow their daily rounds without having the din of clanging swords for ever in their earl. '

div.head: HUSBANDING RESOURCES.
div.p: HUSBANDING RESOURCES.

One of the most important things to bear in mind is that if we are to have complete victory we shall have to husband our resources tea a greater extent than we are doing at pres- ent This is the one point where the Ger- mans, up to now, have beaten us. They have saved and husbanded their resources, and have allowed us to delude ourselves, with the idea that they were starving. While we were rubbing our hands and saying the end was near, they were congratulating them- selves on the fact that their organised economy would enable their poorer, means to outlast our better means that were being lav- ishly and light-heartedly squandered. Locally, steps were taken this week to form a com- mittee to Organise an economy campaign, and we 'earnestly draw the attention of our readers to the arguments that were then placed before. the town by such representative financial ex- perts as the MAYOR, Mr- C. div.head: NO ELECTIONS.

On Thursday the Elections and Registration Bill received the Royal Assent and became law. Under the provisions of this Act the _next statutory elections of county and borough councillors, guardians, and parish councillors will be postponed. for .a year, and the term of office of existing councillors and guardians will be extended by one year. L.G.B. President's Appeal For Voluntary Helpers.

. . div.head: Have You Offered?
div.p: Have You Offered?

It is most important that this work should be conducted as expeditiously as possible, And it is therefore desirable that the local authority should have abundant help for the purpose. The Government are anxious on the one hand that the industrial occupations of the country should not be affected by the preparation of the register, and on the other that the cost should be kept as low as is consistent with efficiency. "For this reason I have suggested," writes the Right Hon. Walter H. Long, the new President of the Local Government Board, "that local authorities should avail themselves to the fullest extent of voluntary assistance in the wort of preparing the register. I have myself received numerous offers of help from all classes—clergy- men, professional men, school teachers, special constables, &c.—and •I am convinced that it is only necessary to inform the public that their help is needed to obtain from them an abund- ance of voluntary service. WORKINGMEN AND THE COMING STRAIN.
"HUSBAND YOUR RESOURCES."
Mr. Geo. Walker's Advice To The Infirmary Committee.

Mr. George Walker, presiding over a meeting of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, held at the Druids' Hall on Wednesday even- ing, at the end of the formal business said he would like to call their attention to a matter which had been causing him grave concern. The financial stress caused by the war would undoubtedly come six or eight months after ' peace had been declared. We should then, he thought, witness times of great difficulty, scarcity and suffering. It behoved every one— every working man, especially—to take the greatest possible .care of his earnings to-day. In these times of full employment and good wages, when labour was in extreme demand we did not pay as much attention to this matter as in normal times. The struggle was not now; it lay in the future. He was recently speaking to the manager of a large works employing 7,000 hands. The gentleman said they were very- busy on war work, but when that was with- drawn and a thousand employes returned from 'the war he would not know what to do. Other firms said the same. His earnest advice to ;working men was to husband their resources now in order to meet the strain that was assuredly coming.

div.p: REV. T. T. JAMES
Writes After A Month Among
The Wounded.
/ In the course of a letter to his congregation the Rev. T. T. James, the pastor of the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, Who is now serving as a chaplain "soracwhere in France," writes

"I have had a month amongst the wounded since last writing you, and have been the whole time in one centre. Very sad it is to see the suffering which this war involves, but very heartening, too, to see the courage and cheer- fulness with which it, is borne. You would be delighted to see the efficiency with which the most serious cases arel dealt with here under canvas, and the complete equipment which has been provided under very difficult circum- stances. On the whole, we have had very little really hot weather, and there has been a con- siderable amount of heavy rain. For this we should probably be grateful, for the moderate temperature has doubtless acted as a real deterrent to ,disease. The great institution out here is the post bag, and I would recommend anyone who wants to do a little bit of really helpful work for the lads at the Front to find time to write letters to them."

div.head: Leather Trade Strong.
div.p: Leather Trade Strong.

The demand for leather, writes— the War: rington correspondent of the "Leather Trades Review," continues to run strongly, and dur- ing the week the call was heavy and the out- put very full. The Leeds Fair brought an in- creased number of buyers to this district, the result being that the warehouses were fairly clear before the end of the week. The search for army, bends was very keen, and apparently manufacturers are finding difficulty in getting enough for current requirements. It is im- possible to increase the number being turned out; indeed, it may even be very difficult to maintain the present rate, as supplies of suit- able hides are becoming much harder to obtain. Other weights of • bends were in full demand. General trade was good, oausing medium-weight lines to move quickly, and there was a growing inquiry for a foreign bend at a relatively low price, and I believe a very fair trade is running in this line. Hide prices had a sensational collapse last week, losing 2d. per lb. in some cases, and with the experience gained it may be doubted if they will again be permitted to go as high as they were; cer- tainly, with export absolutely prohibited, and the market thus in eueown hands, it remains a 'mystery why British tanners pushed up the prices to the extent they did.

div.head: NEED FOR ACTION.
div.p: THE NEED FOR ACTION.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The Grappenhall Detachment of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment had its first drill on Tuesday, the 20th inst., when 18 men put in an appearance, and a second drill on Tuesday last, when 19 Grappenhall men were•present. The number of those who have sent in applica- tions for enrolment is 22.

The question arises, are these figures satis- factory? Personally I consider them most in- adequate. There must be a reason for this apathy of the population amongst the men, and women also. I have tried to trace it, and found many proferred "reasons" why a man should not do his duty to himself, his wife and children, leaving out all idea of duty to country. One " reason " given is that as "A" does not do his duty I do not see why I should, and I will not. Surely a better stand to take would be—"B " does his duty and I will do mine. Another "reason" is—" It will cost me money to buy my uniform, and I have none to spare." This seems plausible, but it is based on a wrong foundation. Poverty is no bar to a man joining us. If a man cannot pay the whole or any part of the cost entailed by doing his hit in the defence of his wife, family and home, the deficiency will be paid for him. Another " reason", is—" I do not see that the Volunteers are any good and are only laughed at, and will never be required as the Germans will not get to Grappenhall." This, to my mind, is the most contemptuous "reason" of all, and shows disloyalty, the • • spirit of the coward, or the cupidity of the imbecile.

Lord Kitchener and the Government call for these Volunteers, and to thwart them is dis- loyalty. Do not let us ask are the Volunteers any good, but rather let us ask are they any harm, and suggest that they may be some good. A man who cannot stand being laughed at for doing his best by those who are doing nothing (but laughing like idiots) cannot be much better than a coward; and a man who can trust to the kindness of the Germans to leave us alone is capable of being duped by the confidence trick. Surely the country has played this game too much in the past. Are we still going on with it?

I, havf; alluded to the apathy among the women. Are they alive to what would hap- pen to them if the enemy were to land on these shores? Have they heard anything about what happened to the women of Belgium? Have they no influence with their husbands and menfolk to shame them into taking their part in the prevention of the horrors of war —on a scale worse than in Belgium? As chairman of the Grappenhall Parish Council, chairman of the committee of the Grappenhall Detachment of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment, a member of the General Committee and of the Finance Committee of the Knutsford Battalion of the same regiment, I am anxious that the men of Grappenhall and district should play an honourable part in the defence of those dear to them, and want to see a platoon (56 men) at least formed, and Ippeal Most earnestly to every man, rich or poor, who does not wish to prove himself a oward or slacker, to cothe forward and join us at our drill in the Large Room on ,Wednes- day next at 7.45 p.m. I appeal to the women to encourage the men to learn how to protect them and be given the right to do so.

The objects of the regiment are : (a) To promote recruiting for the Army. This is the primary duty of all enrolling. 93) To encourage men not of age or other- wise disqualified for service in the Army to drill and learn the elements of musketry in their spare time.

In order to-ensure that we have only in our ranks• mon ineliaible to serve, under the colours, all cases of men wishing to enrol, whO are of eligible age, will be submitted to the Chief Recruiting Officer of the. county. We do not receive men under military age into our ranks unless they are certified by the recruit- ing officer, as having genuine .reasons for not enlisting. The moveinent is under Government recogni- tion and his Majesty the King has accepted' a Volunteer proficiency badge, thus Showing he personal interest in the scheme. The regiment is formed for .homs defence only, and performing this duty we are enabling others to go to the Front—Yours, Zic.,
F. A. FROST. Grappenhall Hall, 3.-tily 30, 1915.

'ALBERT LIGHTFOOT.

Reported Wounded In The Charge, But Was killed. Private Albert Lightfoot, of 4, Furness- street, was reported wounded in the Terri- torial charge upon the German trenches on June 16th but, after a silence of over a month, news has now come to hand that he was killed in action and not wounded. On Thursday night this week Private Lightfoot's parents, Mr. Enoch and Mrs. Margaret Lightfoot, who have recently re- moved to 58, Winwick- street, received a letter from the Territorial Infantry Record Office, Preston, saying that their son, reported wounded, was now re- ported killed in action. "I trust you will derive some consola- tion in knowing , that he fell for A glorious cause and in defence of his country" is the concluding sentence in the sad but sympa- thetic letter.
Perished Nobly. Lieut. Armstrong has also written Mr. and Mrs. Lightfoot. He says : "I have made the fullest possible inquiries regazding your son, but I regret to say, with- outlfuee,ess.
"I am afraid, therefore, that the report of his being wounded is an error, and that he perished nobly on the 16th June. _ • _

„,Knowing him as his company officer, I know that your son would die a true soldier's death, bravely doing his duty for his country. "Kindly accept from myself and the other officers of B Company our heartfelt sympathy in your time of sorrow.—Yours sincerely, W. K. ARMSTRONG, Lieutenant.” A Wycliffe Schoolboy. •

Private Lightfoot, who was twenty years of age last February, the day he entered the trenches, worked as a wiredrawer at White- cross, where his father has been employed for forty years. He went to Wycliffe School as Et boy, and was fond of athletics. He had be- longed to the Territorials two years when the war broke out, and was noted generally for his good character and steady conduct. Prior to the date of the charge his parents heard from him regularly, and the last letter they received from him came three days be- fore that glorious but fatal event, thanking his mother for a parcel she had sent him.

div.head: FRESH FROM TRENCHES.
div.p: FRESH FROM TRENCHES.
More Warrington " Terriers "
Home On Short Leave.
RETICENT HEROES.

Straight from the Front, ten of Warring- ton's brave Territorials arrived in the town, on short home-leave, on Sunday afternoon, in- cluded in their number being a few Sergeants. Their train steamed into Bank Quay Station shortly before 4 o'clock, and, as news of their coming had not been trumpeted abroad, there was only a comparatively small crowd—mainly consisting of relatives and friends—to greet them. Bronzed of complexion the men looked, physically, as they wo-Od themselves phrase it, "in the pink," but their uniforms bore traces of the rigours of trench life and cam- paigning generally. Every man had "the soldier's best friend," -his rifle, with him, as well as practically the whole of the full cam- paigning kit, barring, of course, their ground sheets, blankets, &c.

div.head: AFFECTING RE-UNIONS.
div.p: AFFECTING RE-UNIONS.

Most of the re-unions between the brave lads and their relatives were of a decidedly affect- ing nature, and after their kinsmen and kins- women had finished shaking their hands and embracing them, respectively, the friends and the souvenir hunters crowded round, and one by one the lads were cajoled into parting with

little mementos of the battlefield—i spent cart- ridge here, a fragment of shell there, a tarnished button somewhere else; and so on! They were also speedily relieved of the neces- sity of carrying their belongings; it was an
honour that many strove for allowed to act as honorary light porter to the bonnie lads.

In one instance the "best girl"—or was it only a sister—shouldered a braw soldier's rifle and in another a "wee bit lassie" struggled man- full under the weight of the substantial military great coat.

div.head: SOME OF THE WAITING PEOPLE DISAPPOINTED.
div.p: SOME OF THE WAITING PEOPLE DISAPPOINTED.

To some of the bronzed, boyishly-happy men the homecoming was specially joyous, for the expectant throng included for them a delir- iously joyous wife and unrestrainedly-excited "kiddies." Some of the women in the wait- ing crowd who had arrived with hearts full of hope, left with tear-dimmed eyes, for their "boys," they found, had not been included in the home-leave draft—riot yet! And there was one black-garbed lady hovering in the rear of the press that surged round the re- turned heroes—are they not all heroes?—whose heart was not buoyed up by hope of a material kiss and a warm handclasp from the one she loved so dearly, for she knew that her son had shed his life's blood in the gallant charge that has given the Warrington "Terriers" an honoured place in the annals of military his- tory for all time. All she wanted was more news of her boy; a story that told her in more detail than the bald cold print of the official notification how her boy had made the supreme sacrifice for King and country.

div.head: ARRIVALS AND DEPARTURES!
div.p: ARRIVALS AND DEPARTURES!

As the train bearing the ten "Terriers" drew up .at one platform ,in the station, another train steamed in at another, convey- ing to the South several hundreds of newly- trained warriors who were on their way to ieceive their baptism of fire. And it says 'some- thing for the spirit of the Britisher ,that the Men who were "off to go through it" were every whit as cheerful and as happy as the men who had been through it. Those who had seen "it" exchanged handshakes and good wishes with those who are going to see "it," and, somehow, one felt equally proud of both seta of lads.

div.head: NOT DOWNHEARTED YET!
div.p: NOT DOWNHEARTED YET!

The returned " Tommies" were vivacious conversationalists when it came to recounting their experiences to their admiring relatives and friends, but they "shut up," 'like the proverbial oyster, when a Pressman ap- proached them. "We mustn't say anything!" one of them told an "Examiner" repreeenta- tive. "Those are our instructions—we are not to say where we have been and we are to tell the newspapers nothing they don't already know about the fighting. You can say this, however, on behalf of all the War- rington bhoys' at the Front that we are 'not downhearted yet'—not a single mother's son of us, and, what's more, there's pot a single one of us that regrets the day he put his name down for active service. We're proud to have had a hand in thiS big game and we think every fit young man, who is not a.ctuully needed at home, ought to come out and 'have a packet at it' with os.. And then it would 'be soon over !"

div.head: Al AT LLOYD'S.
div.p: Al AT LLOYD'S.

"What do .we think of the ' Frenchies'"? the speaker added in answer to a tentative question by an euvesdropper, "They're Al at Lloyd's, and their women and children didn't half make a fuss of us wherever we stopped on our way to -- well ~the place where we sailed from. They couldn't do enough for us, but the war hasn't left them much to do it with. The people *of England vtpuld go down on their knees in thanks•every hour of"the day if they only knew. .how much happier and easier is their lot, as compared with that of the in- habitants of the parts we have been. in. Give you my word,, there isn't much picture show and beer and billiards about the Belgians and the French people this weather r'

div.head: "THAT CHARGE WAS A DO'!"
div.p: "THAT CHARGE WAS A DO'!"

"Was I in the charge?" the speaker--qnite one of the most elderly of the little group of returned heroes—continued, "01 course, I was in the charge. You didn't think I would miss a share in the biggest thing we have done, did you? That charge was a do,' I can tell you, and all of us that came through it may think I ourselves lucky' chaps. But there 7-- I didn't. want to talk about it. I'm here to enjoy myself for a day or two and the `missus' wants to get me home. Besides didn't I tell you that I mustn't say anything to reporters. You see, they can cross things they don't want you to know out of our letters, but they couldn't censor our tongues, if they gave us leave to talk at all freely." Another of the returned warriors laid stress on the joy it gave the men in the trenches to receive parcels, letters and newspapers from home. "If you only knew what it was like out there" he said, "you would see why we think such a lot of those things. Why, we are like 'kids' going to• a Sunday school pic- nic when we get anything from our people!" The leave of the men who came on Sunday expired on Thursday afternoon.

div.head: COLONEL FAIRCLOUGH. An Interrupted Leave Of Absence.
div.p: COLONEL FAIRCLOUGH. An Interrupted Leave Of Absence.

Colonel B. Fairclough, commanding the War- rington Territorials on active service, was to have arrived home on Monday on leave for a few days; but circumstances arose whioh pre- vented his coming. He is entitled to a rest and a shange after the strenuous labours through which he has lately passed, and it is hoped he will be able to take that rest at no distant date.

Corporal Joseph Harcourt Tombs, whose conspicuous gallantry has gained him the most enviable honour the British Army has to offer to its sons, is a native of Melbourne, Australia. div.head: V.C.'s VISIT TO OLD WORKPLACE.
div.p: V.C.'s VISIT TO OLD WORKPLACE.
An Informal Call To Shake Hands And Say "Thank You."

Without giving‘the slightest warning of his intention to do so, Corporal Tombs on Wednesday morning paid a brief visit to the Aiuminium Works at Bank Quay—the place where he was employed when the outbreak of war called him to the colours. He had put in about eighteen months in these works, and he had formed many friendships among his fellow employes, more especially those in the sheet- metal department, where he was himself en- gaged. By those over him he was regarded as a very useful and dependable worker, whilst his equals always voted him "a good chap." "lie was a fellow one could get on with," a fellow worker, who knows the V.C. hero well, told our representative. "There was nothing swanky' about him, but he always gave one the idea of having plenty of grit' and pluck. He was always ready to do a 'pal' a good turn. We are proud to think that we have worked with him." An Unexpected Pleasure:

It was about 11.30 in the morning when the plucky Corporal strolled up to the works gates, and after a cheery word with an old 'workmate, who chanced to, be close by, made his way to the office, and inquired for the manager. That gentleman lost- no time in receiving his distinguished visitor, and the pair exchanged a hearty hapdshake. The Corporal was modesty itself; he abso- lutely declined to be lionised, or to talk about himself and his deed of imperishable gallan- try. He just wanted, he said, to say " Thank you!" to the manager, and through him to , the proprietors of the works, for what had be ) 1 done, financially, for him and his de- pendents during the time he had been on active service. He desired to leave as unos- tentatiously as he had come, but he was not suffered to go until he had promised to pay another and more ceremonial visit to the works, in order that his old workmates might have the opportunity of showing their appre- ciation of his great pluck. This visit he has promised to pay before he goes back to the Front.

Quietly as the Corporal had entered the works, his departure was by no means un- observed, for somehow, after the wonderful way that news does travel, tidings that he was about had got abroad, and when he left to go to see the Mayor there was quite a con- siderable knot of people round the gates, and he took his leave to the accompaniment of the clicking of camera-shutters and a good hearty round of cheers.

In the forenoon Of Wednesday Corporal Tombs, accompanied by Mr. Stewart, of the British Aluminium Co., called upon the Town Clerk, who got into instant communication with the Mayor and several other accessible members of the Council. In a few minutes there assembled in the Mayor's Parlour, in:
addition to his Worship and the Town Clerk, Aldermen Smethurst, Tinnion and Bennett, and Councillor Roberts.
A bottle of wine was opened and the toasts of the King and of Corporal Tombs were drunk.
Corporal Tombs, who drank a temperance drink, told his story modestly and intelli- gently to his hosts, who were keenly inter- ested in all he had to say..

The Mayor said he, v-ias• pleased to be the chief 'magistrate of ai town that was repre- sented in the Army by such a hero as Corporal Tombs. He appreciated Corporal Tombs's call almost as soon as he arrived in Warring- ton, and 'while it was difficult to say at the moment what recognition should be made of the event, he thought, if ' Corporal Tombs could arrange it, the people of Warrington would be glad to see a live IT.C. in their midst, I and he would -be glad to provide for a public reception and procession on Saturday (to-day). To this Corporal Tombs agreed and intim- ated that after he had been to London to see the directors of the British Aluminium Co., and to transact other business, he would re- turn to Warrington in time for the reception and procession proposed by the Mayor. In order to meet the extraordinary expenses the visit must put him to in the peculiar cir- cumstances, Corporal Tombs was presented by the Town Clerk from a fund available for the purpose with £lO,

div.head: DISAPPOINTMENT IN HOWLEY' LANE.
div.p: DISAPPOINTMENT IN HOWLEY- ' LANE.

When it was known that Corporal Tembs was in town it was naturally inferred that he would visit his home in Howley-lane' and the residents of that busy thoroughfare bedecked their house fronts and bent forth'garlands in all directions. div.head: CORPORAL'S OWN STORY.
div.p: THE CORPORAL'S OWN STORY.
Rescuing For Hours And Was
Not Scratched.
Special " Examiner " Interview.

An "Examiner" representative had an interview with Corporal Tombs at the offices of the British Aluminium Company, Ltd., at Bank Quay. He found him looking fairly "fit," but evidently on the tired side, which, of course, was latt to be wondered at, seeing the long journey he had just completed. The Corporal seemed more willing to talk about the many congratulations he had received on the honour he had *on than of the brave deeds which led to its award. It was only towards the end of the interview that he was induced to talk about them, and as this part is the most important, we put what he said first. "On the Saturday night," he said, "we went straight out, and as soon as day broke the fun' started, and it was hell itself. They must have fired at us every conceivable kind of shell. Going back, I spotted one of the chaps badly hit, and I brought him in. I saw another, and could not rest, so fetched him in. I had been out a second time, and now made a third attempt. I said, Here's

lanother go.' I was determined to get this other chap in. He was groaning. The first shelter I could spot I was in, and looked for my man and got hold of him. My word, he was hit, tot). Captain Norris passed a re- mark about it. He said, 'Well, it's a wonle - the chap's alive.' I got this chap in, and I saw another out,, very badly hit. He called, ' For God's sake, get me in if you can.' I shouted 'Buck up l' I got a couple of rifle slings, fastened them together round the back of my neck, and under his arms and we made a break for it. How we got in I don't know. I didn't get a scratch. All this took a matter of hours. The first man took three-quarters of an hour. You had to crawl out and in as best you could." , Asked when he got his promotion from lance-corporal to corporal, Tombs said that when the colonel heard of what he had done he.said he was to be a full corporal.

and (when the war broke out) for the British Aluminium Co., Ltd. The large number of firms by whom he was employed during a sojourn of only a few years in Warrington is an indication of the restless and roviiig nature of his character.
