div.head: GREAT NEWS.
div.p: THE GREAT NEWS.
"How Aid you. get the news about the

_ Corporal Tombs spoke freely now, and told at some length how the good news reached him. He said he was nicely asleetrin his dug- out when a " chap " came along calling" Cor- poral Tombs !" He asked him what he wanted, and he replied "Come along, I have some good news for you. I said I would bring you some good news some time." Tombs told him to "go on," he Was "telling the tale." But in a few minutes Captain Ryan came round and said, "Tombs, allow me to congrat- ulate you," handing him an Army telegram, -reading "Please inform Corporal Tombs he has been awarded the V.C."

div.head: "ARE YOU TOMBS'?"
div.p: "ARE YOU TOMBS'?"

" I thanked him and all the rest of it," pro- ceeded the Corporal, "and then Mr. Marsh, who had joined just recently, said 'Oh, are you Tombs?' I said, Yes, sir, I am,' and saluted him. He said Put it there (holding his hand out) and allow me to congratulate you. You deserve not only the V.C., but something behind it.' Others came along and said I &served it, had worked hard for it, and they were glad I had got it. Mr. Harvey, 2nd lieutenant, who has always taken a particular interest in me, and to whom I showed the letters I have had from Mr. W. Murray Mor- rison, general manager of the British Aluminium Co., also came along and said I was exceedingly lucky, the firm would be mak- ing me one of the directors. After that the boys came along and made a great fuss." Corporal Tombs went on to tell of the many congratulations he got. One was from Cor- poral Richardson, who; he said, got his arm up and swung him round the neck, saying "You deserve it; you cannot tell how pleased I am. When you get home you won't forget to write me and go and see mother."

div.head: "REGIMENT IS PROUD OF YOU."
div.p: "REGIMENT IS PROUD OF YOU."

Corporal Tombs was instructed to see the adjutant about getting leave. When the ad- jutant saw him he was all smiles and said, "Well, Corporal Tombs what is it?" " I said I would like to thank Colonel Stevenson for what he has done in getting me this die. tinction." He laughed and leaned back read- ing a newspaper, and "when he got up he didn't half get hold of me," said the Corporal. "He nearly pulled my arm off. He said 'I am proud of -you, your regiment is proud of you. You are the first man in it to get the V.C. We cannot tell you how proud we are of you. At first I was afraid it would be only the D.C.M., but fortune has favoured you, and you have got the highest honour.' " On his way to the boat at Boulogne, Cor- poral Tombs met some "Navy boys." ,One said, t‘ Hello, ginger, I see you have done it at last." "Done what?" asked Tombs, to which the Navy man said, "No beating about the bush. My word, we are proud of you. The boys are over there getting something to eat. Come and join us." The Corporal went "over there," and wanted to pay, but was promptly told to keep his hand out of his pocket. From Boulogne Corporal Tombs sailed to Folkestone, and reached Warrington shortly after ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. He telephoned to Mr. Stewart at the Aluminium Works, and was cordially invited to go down at once. This he did, and was heartily wel- comed by Mr. Stewart and his old workmates.

div.head: REMARKABLE DARING.
div.p: REMARKABLE DARING.

Officer Says Tombs Did The Impos- sible Four Times. A staff officer of the Infantry Brigade with which' the Liverpool Regiment were serving on June 16th, says : " I was an eye-witness of the daring of Tombs, and had I been able to stop him I would have done so, for, to all appearance, the thing he did four times in succession was an impossibility. There had been some hard fight- ing, and an attack 'we made could not be pressed home. In the retirement a lot of our wounded were left behind. Some of them were near enough to cry for help to the trench where Tombs was. • , Walked Into a Pitiless Fire. "In front of the trench there was a pitiless ' fire from the enemy's big guns and a number of machine guns, while riflemen were posted only two hundred yards away picking off any- thing they could Dee. Into this walked the solitary figure of a man we afterwards found to be Tombs. He looked for a moment as though he hadn't quite made up his mind what to do. But finally he cleared the space between him and the nearest wounded with a rush, and was seen to throw _himself beside a man. "At first we feared he had been hit, but a minute or two later we saw him move cautiously towards his own trench, and by his side was one of the wounded, whom he helped along as best he could. It still rained bullets from the machine guns,-;,,and shrapnel was bursting at short intervals, and bullets whistled perilously near. At one stage Tombs had to carry his companion on his back and make a run for it, but they got through all right. "Then he reappeared, and began the perilous journey over again. This time his companion did not seem to be.badly hit, for he went along in a stooping position beside Tombs, and occasionally they broke into a run, only looking around now and then to judge the direction of coming shells. They got through. Death Staring Him in the Face. "And once more the solitary figure began that journey with death staring him in the face at every step. It was some time before he got hold of another wounded man, and when they started they seemed to be walking on their hands and knees. This must have been the time when Tombs dragged in the wounded man with the aid of a rifle sling. After they had gone some distance the enemy's fire became heavier, and the two men had to take shelter in a shell hole But soon they started off again, and got safely through. "For the fourth time Tombs appeared over the parapet and made the risky journey. By now the movements had apparently been seen from the German' lines, for-the hidden riflemen began to fire rapidly, and the macliine guns rained bullets by the thousand. Tombs dis- appeared from view, and we thought he had gone, but later he reappeared; accompanied by another man, and the two picked their wiy painfully hick. Then they disappeared over the parapet."

div.head: "GERMANS MOWED US DOWN."
div.p: "GERMANS MOWED US DOWN."
Corporal Writes Of Charge In Which He Won Cross.

M. 1. R. Stewart, of the British Aluminium Company's works, in response to a letter written by him to the plucky corporal, received the following letter : " Dear Mr. Stewart,—l am very pleased to say that I am the Tombs referred to in the papers. lau sure you will be pleased with the news. My cousin told me all about it; how she was told the news by Mr. Spinks, at the Parr Hall. Well, sir, all I say is that I only did my duty. But, my word, I never wish to see another engage- ment like it. It was like hell itself ! Shrap- nel, lyddite, and machine gun fire swept the
whole place. I saw two stretcher-arers and a wounded man blown to piecea Twenty yards from where I was bandaging a chap up.

"Proud to Bring Credit upon the Firm." "In the last charge that we made on the Wednesday the Germhuns moved Us down as we broke through the opening in the captured trench. The sights were awful! One poor chap close to ms and my chum was riddled—he looked as if rats had been nibbling at him on one side. It was the machine guns that had done it, and his tunic was in ribbons—ripped by the bullets. My Commanding Officer sent for me the other day and told me that he had recom- mended me for the V.C., and even if I don't get that, I am sure of the D.C. Medal. One thing more, sir! lam pleaset, to say that the 'British Aluminium Co.'s men have done their share out• here, and as an -employe of the company I am proud to be able to bring credit upon it." The V.C. hero adds that writing paper is very scarce in the trenches, and finishes with "kind regards to all at the mill" and to Mr. Stewart.
C.S.M.'s HIGH PRAISE.
"I Am Proud to Have Him in My Zompany."
Company-Sergeant-Major W. J. Ilea- 05- ,of the Ist King's (Liverpool), writes Mr. Stftwart as follows :

"Corporal Tombs, of my company, has shown me a letter from you asking him if it is he who has been mentioned as doing great and good work. He brought in four or five wounded men on improtsed stretchers, and I sincerely hope tbat he has been awarded the Victoria Cross, which, in my opinion, he richly deserves. I can say that he is recommended for that most coveted prize, and that he is an excellent asset to the Army, and a man whom I am proud to have in my company." _ _ "Dear Mr. Stewart,—l am pleased to say I am the Lance-Corporal Tombs to whom reference is made. Company-Sergtant-
Major Heaps, my C.S.M., will bear ou-t the facts referred to. I showed him your letter _ _ . _

and my Company Officer (Mr. test) also, both of whom were pleased, and I take :the liberty to thank you on behalf of my regi- ment also for the praise you attribute to us. . . . I can assure you we had a het time of it, but we came off victorious. Itr. Last led us in the charge, and, I'm pled to say, came back safe and sound when we were relieved on the Wednesday evening. I also wish to thank you on behalf of my cousin for the company's continued itilier- osity. . Kindly remember me to-Tall at the works and accept my kind regards to you and yours.—Yours gratefully, Ritgeph

H. Tomb." In a postscript the writer added: "I Save been promoted to full corporal since last writing. Address: No. 10079 Corporal J. H. Tombs, B Company, Ist Battalion, the King's (Liverpool Regiment), 13-.E.F., c/o London."

div.head: NATIONAL THRIFT.
div.p: NATIONAL THRIFT.
War's Appalling Waste of
Material Resources.

Last Sunday at the Stockton Heath Adult School, a lecturette was given by Mr. W. Row- land on the problem of "Thrift." The lecturer p,ointed out that the coat of a war could not be understood merely from add- ing together the various national budgets. Destruction of pyoperty seldom figured in any national accounts, yet loss of this ,kind was, of course, enormous. A third form of wastage was to be found in -loss of trade and loss, of _pro- duction. Millions of men could not be diverted from productive work without cutting off enor- mous supplies of goods, which otherwise would have been made. Even the slaughter and maiming of men could be estimated in terms of financial loss. Actuaries had calculated that every soldier killed in the course of the war was worth from .2800 to £l,OOO to the com- munity. Besides all this there was ' the depreciation of money values to be considered. The demand for goods and services had gone up at the same time that supplies had gone down, so that the purchasing power of a sovereign was decreasing. But while national expenditure was huge the whole expenditure was not less. Millions of men, women and children were being main- tained by the belligerent States of Europe and vast sums were being spent- in wages for Government work, which circulated round and caused a demand for all sorts of industrial pro- ducts But when all these mitigating circum- stances were taken into account there remained a wastage of material resources that was appall- ing, and of which no adequate conception-could be given. As a. result of the war there will be less =pi, tal to expend on the extension of industry. There will be less money available foiluxuries, and certain trades will ultimately feel the pinch in reduced profits and less employment. Customers will be far poorer in most parts of the civilised world and the effective demand for goods. will be reduced. _ _ _

- The lecturer went on to say that thrift was not merely.. saving. It is the quality which enables a man to produce well and to expend wisely. There were ways in which each in- dividual could take a share in helping the nation.

1. By steady work and good workmanship. These viete always national assets, but they were more needed now than ever before. Strikes and lock-outs, had - time-keeping and careless workmanship, all meant loss to the community in material wealth.
2. Waste of labour ought to be avoided: When the nation was crying out for necessaries we ought not to• dcmand service which- we .can do without. •

3. Simple living would help the State. We must stop our demand for flunkeys, acrobats, .-Oofessional footballers to do our bidding. 'lt ,might be well if there were a tax upon -amuse- ments. The Government had asked people to eat less meat. We must adapt ourselves and find, good substitutes for flesh diet. 4. Wise expenditure was the best kind of economy. It ,did .not mean always linying the cheapest • things. ,Intelliient buying meant. securing:goed value in the shop and extracting' good value after things had been .bought. 5. Banking was also a real help to the -Government. The savings of the people were thus put to the greatest advantage. The man who hoards money in the house is robbing the community.

6. Prompt payment of accounts is another form of communal economy. The credit system was, of course, essential to moderii Commence. But between retail customers and the shopkeepers long credit wa,,, a nuisance and was costly to the community. If the shopkeeper had to wait for his money he could not buy to the best advan- tage from middleman or manufacturer. Where long credit prevailed, goods were more expen- sive, because credit, like all other conveniences, had to be paid for. Book-keeping, debt-collect- ing and bad debts had to be paid for by some- one, but, .a. great deal of this expensive machinery Might be clime away with if people 'chose. .
A Mild Yearn. "Understand," concludexi the struggling young lawyer, -" I hold no brief for the trust." Arid then he added softly.: -"I wish L did„"

There was a discussion at Monday evening's 'meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council as to the shooting rights round the dam. Councillor Lockyer was down to move: "That the shooting round the Dam be let by tender, and that such tender be advertised for." When he rose, in accordance with the notice of motion, hawever. he said he begged to move that the Council let the shooting rights on and around the lake.
The Chairman (Councillor Gotobed) pointed out that what Councillor Lockyer now moved was not the same as the motion on the agenda. Nothing was said about "on" the lake; only " round " was mentioned.
Councillor Lockyer said he meant on as well as round the lake.
The Chairman said he was afraid Councillor Loekyer would have to keep to the original motion.
Council Should "Make Something" Out of the Shooting.

Coun. Warburton said he thought it was Only right and proper that the Council Should be making something out of the shooting on and about the lake. They had had it some time and they ought to do something with it. They had spent thousands of pounds on the lake and round it, and not drawn a penny for it yet. Councillor I.fockyer said he wanted to include the water as well as the land, as it was one of the best ways of getting a good bit of shooting-, particularly in the winter, when the lake was frozen.

div.head: UNJUSTIFIABLE EXPENDITURE."
div.p: UNJUSTIFIABLE EXPENDITURE."
Council And Increase In Cost Of Higher Education.
At Monday evening's meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council a discussion occurred on the subjee,t of the CheOire County Coun- cil's latest effort to raise the rate for higher education.

The Chairman (Councillor R. H. Gotobed) said he and the Vice-Chairman and the Clerk had just come from a Local Government Board inquiry at Crewe, at which the Cheshire County Council had asked the Board for per- raiseion to set about raising a further rate of 2211. for higher education. In view of the fact that 'there was not time to call a meeting of the Council, he thought it his duty to attend the inquiry, in company with the Vice-Chair- man (Councillor Holt) and the Clerk, and offer opposition, on behalf of that Council, to what they considered,. unjustifiable expendi- ture at the present tithe. The meeting was not very protracted, and there was strong opposi- tion. He had to leave the inquiry before the Vice-Chairman, in order to get to the meeting of the Finance Committee, which had just been held downstairs. He left CounciHor Holt at the inquiry on the understanding that he would speak if he had-the opportunity.
' Lymm Strongly Objected To Another Rise.'

Councillor Holt said that all he waa able to say was that they at Lymm strongly objected to another increase in the education rate at the present time. They, as Urban District Councillors, did not know enough of, nor follow enough, the eipenditure being incurred by the County .Council. One of the arguments brought forward was this: This rate was sd. in the pound, and it's gone up to 1(kl., and we have got the money without any difficulty. Novi, why shouldn't we have another *I.? He (Councillor Holt) came away with the im- pression that the money was spent just like water, and with the feeling that they, as Urban, District Councillors, ought to watch more closely the expenditure of the County Council, over which- they had very little con- trol. To take one item: £1,600 had been paid in one year iq travelling expenses of children going from the rural districts to the secondary schools. A lot of figures were given at the in- quiry, but there was little chance of comment- ing on them. During the last three years the sum of £139,310 had been spent on new build- ings. .

div.head: Do Peopill Get Their Money's Worth?
div.p: Do Peopill Get Their Money's Worth?

Councillor Cowper expressed himself as very pleased that the Chairman, Vice-Chairman and Clerk ,had atirded the inquiry. Councillor Holt had give some figures that would open the eyes of many people. Considering what the cast was, he really failed to see where the money's worth came in, and he felt that it was about time business men had a say in the 'hat- ter.

The Chairman said that in the Lymm area they did not contribute any of the amount paid yearly for travelling expenses. They used to, but the amount became so heavy that they were eventually relieved of it. He knew of one skhool where, despite the fact that the number of scholars had dwindled. from sixty to twenty, the full staff of telichers remained. It involved a big waste of money. The thing was&in these times, to see how little could be spent and not how much. Councillor Holt said the Chairman and him- self and the Clerk were not prepared to go into thinute details.
On the koposition of Coun. Parker, the Coun- cil sanctioned the Chairman's action in the matter of the inquiry.

div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
"RESTING 13' AFTER "HOT TIME."

The -local members of the sth Cheshire Ter- ritorials left the trenches on Saturday, after a stay of about a .week and a half, and are .at present "resting" a considerable distance be- hind the firing line in wooden huts. . Corporal Fred Kay, whose home is in Rush Green, and who we stated last week had been slightly wounded, is already back again with them. The other three who were wounded— Private Harry Kay, Private Hadden (of Sta- tham), and Private John Thomason—have, how- ever, not been quite so fortunate, for they are qill in hospital. All, however, are going on well.

In a letfer written by Private Joseph Clare, of Booth's Hill, on Saturday, it is stated: "The Germans have not bothered us with Shells these last two days, and we can do very well without them. Had you the luck to see a Brookes while he was on furlough? I don't suppose he would spend much time in Lymm, his home-being at Wilmslow; but he would visit as many friends as he could." . .

div.head: Met Roland Dixon.
div.p: Met Roland Dixon.

Two days ago -a communication received from Private J. Clare ran: "After leaving the trenches the first Place we got to we stayed the night in huts, and while there I went in, the village, and who should I. see but Roland Dixon! He is in the R.A.M.C. He has only been out a week. What do you think he asked? If lye had been in the trenches yet! Sorry to hear of Fred Daniels being killed. I think Lymm is having its share of casualties, but after all is said and done, it speaks well for the little village—so many answering the country's call. We have done well this trip, for there was for each one of us a tin of pineapple and cocoa from Lymm that the scholars of the Grammar School had collected for us."

div.head: Lymm Men Dwindling.
div.p: Lymm Men Dwindling.

Writing to Miss Bessie Cross, of Bridgewater- street, on the 20th, Private Percy Clare said: "We are still in the trenches; we are expecting; to be relieved next Saturday night. lam send- ing this letter by H. Brookes, as he is leaving the trenches for home to-morrow (Wednesday); he will post this in England [at Cheadle; his home]. We had a rather hot time yesterday, as the Germans were shelling us all day.. We have only been in three days, and have lost about thirty or forty men. I never saw any- thing like it before; shells were dropping all about us—in front of the trench, behind, and in the trench. We got five wounded out of our platoon. One was a chap that you would not know; he was not a Lymm chap. I am sorry to say he is dead; he died in the night. He had about five wounds in his back, poor chap. The other four were Lymm lads—Lance-Corporal F. Kay and his brother H. Kay, W. Hadden and Jack Thomason. It was rather funny; it was the first time in the trenches for W. Hadden and J. Thomason. All the four were slightly wounded. . . . Two came, out with our re- inforcements from Lymm,- and they have gone back wounded so soon—they had only been with us about, two weeks. We shall not have many

from Lymm soon. . . . The Germand are a bit better this morning, but we never know when they are going to start. . . . R. Percival is all right again. He is with us in the trenches; he was only asking me the ether day how Arthur is going on." "Like Drunken Men, Failing."

Yesterday Mr. D. Daniels, confectioner, of Booth's Hill, received the following letter: "We have left the place where we have been staying the last three months. We left on Saturday night, and did a march of about ten miles. Then we had a few hours' rest, and at about half-past seven at night set out again. We were on the mar6h till two o'clock next morn- ing. Talk about drunken men! We were worse, falling all over the road; we were all dead beat and ready for a good sleep. We have got a good billet in a little French village. It has -a stone 'floor, but we can sleep as well as in any bed. We were all glad to get in a place with a roof on it. It is a month or two now since we have had a place to go in—it has either been the trenches or the field. Thank God, we are no worse for it yet! It is for a good cause! I think we are leaving here sometime this week." Marched Eighty Miles.

Writing on Sunday to his mother, Mrs. G. Davies, Private Percy Clara said: "We are out of the trenches again. We got relieved soon after 9 o'clock last night, and we were on the march till about 3 o'clock this mornins. _We
arc on our way to France—it is about—eighty-

miles from the trenches we have been in. We are in wooden huts just for to-day; we move off from here at about 6 o'clock.ta-night—another good march! Then I think we are having a few days' rest, and then we are entraining. I think it will be two or three weeks before we go in any trenches again—it may be longer. We were glad to get down after our march, but now we have had a rest we are ready for an- other march. . . . I had -a lucky 'do' this time in the trenches, when they were shelling us. I got a piece of shell in my belt; it cut the cloth on my back. . . ."

div.head: HOME FROM THE TRENCHES.
div.p: HOME FROM THE TRENCHES.

Private Henry Brookes paid a visit to Lymm last week, during_ the course or a furlough from the trenches. Leaving France on Wednesday morning, he arrived at his own home at Cheadle the following morning,, remaining there a day. On the Friday evening he reached the home of his mother, Mrs. James Taylor at 1, West Hyde, Lymm. Then followed two busy days, during which he visited friends of his own and his comrades in all parts of the village, and he left on Sunday afternoon, leaving for the 1 Front again on Monday morning. Out therl, he serves as a highly-valued stretcher-hearer. Private Brookes "looked splended, and was in the hest of health." 'Private James 'Taylor—who is the brother of Private Brookes—has also visited his :home. This he did on Friday evening of last week, coming from-.,Lineoln -County -Hospital. where be --has•-been - since March .26th. He was tlie first Lymm Territorial :wounded, • and is still Without 'the -use of _ his left arm, thoitgli_ile hopes for the best, as he :remain in pail for two or three months yet. lie is in the best of spirits.

div.head: PERSONAL NOTES.
div.p: PERSONAL NOTES.

Private James Leah, who is lying ill in the 16th General Hospital, Letreport, France, ,writes to his wife at The Rookery, Booth's Hill -1 "I am a lot better than I was. . . . I ant' sorry to hear of Fred Daniels being killed. . . . I may be sent to England when I get fit to. travel—it may be in a week's time or a fortnight's; it just depends on how soon I get better. . . I have had to be moved to an- other ward. They live saved my life, because if they had not moved me and done for me what they did, I should have been a dead man to- day:"

Private Leah's ease was an unfortunate one, as he was taken ill three weeks ago, the day before he should have started home on a five day? furlough, after being,at the Front since February. Private Stanley Gibbs, who was wounded in the left hand on May 11th, is progressing very well in the Toxteth Park Military Hospital. R,eoently he underwent an operation,- a---bone being extracted :fromhis arm and:scraped. The operation -was 'successfully -performed. Private Gibbs does not yet know how long he will be before cominc home.

Private William Jackson, of 3, Moston-street, who is the youngesMspm " Terrier " and who was wounded in the !eft leg, has made good progress at the Banstead Military Hospital, and is expected home to-day for a week's stay before going to join his regiment at Chester. Last week his brother Harry joined the King's Royal Rifle,s.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS' DIFFICULTY.
div.p: VOLUNTEERS' DIFFICULTY.
Bank Holiday Orders Clash With
Inspection Programme.

Latest battalion orders to the Lymm platoon of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment are to the effect that the battalion shall assemble at Mere on Monday morning at 11.15. Presumably the purpose is inanceurres. It had previously been planned—and the transport had been ordered accordingly—that the Corps should be conveyed to Altrincham Station, there to entrain for Chester—where an inspection was to take place by General Sir 01'core .Creagh, at Roodee. This arrange- ment may, of course, yet be carried out; as the difficulty is not insurmountable.
This week J. T. Milne has qualified as a marksman in the Corps, musketry—with a scare of 95 deliberate and 90 rapid. Mr. Mime is the oldest member of the C2ri..s. • •

div.head: PRIVATE WALTER HADDEN.
div.p: PRIVATE WALTER HADDEN.
Describes How The Casualties Occurred.
Private Walter Hadden, of Statham Cross- ings—who was wounded in the palm of his right hand—writes to his mother at Pepper- street :

"I have been discharged from hospital, and have been sent down to a convalescent camp at .Rouen. I was only in the hospital at Letreport five days, and should have liked to be sent home; but it was not my luck some- how. I cannot tell you how long I shall be here, as my hand is getting better very nicely and I have got the use of my fingers again, and have had the piece of shrapnel taken out. When I am fit again I am going back to the trenches, and I do not think it will be long before I am back again among the shot and shell. I have. christened 'Jack Johnson's' 'coalboxes '—as they don't. half come with a rattle, and burst like thunder, and the holes they make in the ground you could put a horse and cart in.

- How was it I got hit? I had been in the dug-outs with Ernest and J. Gilbert having a sleep. When it came daylight the Gentians started to shell the trenches where we were and it woke us up. So J. Gilbert said 'Here, I'm going put of this row, and I followed him; and I hadn't hardly got out of the dug-outs and was just going to ask J. Thomason for .a drink of tea kwhich he had only just made in the trenches) when one of the coalboxes ' came sailing over our heads and burst just be- hind us. And the shrapnel caught J. Thomason and -11. Kay and me; but I am glad to tell you they are only slight wounds. I don't know where J; Thomason and H. Kay have gone with their wounds, as I left them in the hospital at Letreport, but I hope they have the luck to get to England, as it is awful out here.

div.head: " I Dropped On Pals."
div.p: " I Dropped On Pals."

"I had only been here an hour before I dropped on two pals who asked me whether I used to play goal for Lymm, so I told them I did. One of them was a Latchford player, and the other was Arthur Foy-e from Altrincham; plenty of Lymm people know him, as he used to play goal for Oughtrington Park. So we had a good talk together about the fine times we have had when we went footballing, and then we went together to see the pictures, which are on the camp ground; we spent a nice evening. He is in the same regiment as me; it was funny that two goalkeepers should meet one another!

"I sleep in the next bed to the chap from Latchford. He belongs to the Warrington regiment. "I was surprised to drop on John Skelhorn out here; he is in the same camp as me. He is in the First _Cheshire Regiment, and told me he had been through the Battle of Mons. He has had all his front teeth knocked out by shrapnel, and he isn't going back to the trenches again. . . . Our Ernest was all right when I left him."

div.head: PRIVATE HARRY KAY.
div.p: PRIVATE HARRY KAY.
In Same French Hospital As Another
Comrade.

Private Harry Kay, whose home is at Yew Tree-terrace, Rush Green, was wounded in the left arm by a piece of shrapnel from the same shell as wounded his brother, Lance-Corporal Fred Kay. In fact, all the four Lymm lads wounded last week, as well as the Birkenhead private who was killed, were hurt by the same shell.

Private Kay, now lies in the Canadian Hospital at Letreport—the same as Private George Tay- lor. Private Kay writes to his mother to say ,that he is doing very well, and does not think he will get to England unless a big battle takes place and the hospital is required for large batches of newly wounded. Mrs. Kay has also received word from her son, Private Tom Kay, of the R.A.M.C., saying that he visited the convalescent camp where he had heard his brother, Lance-Corporal Fred Kay (of the Lymm Territorials), was, but found he had just been discharged, and had rejoined his regi- merit to do light duties. The Lance-Corporal was bruised in the back, foot, and ankle, but happily not seriously injured.

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN THOMASON.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN THOMASON.
Arrives In England And Tells How He
Was Saved.

Good news comes to hand respecting Private John Thomason, of New-road, Lymm Bridge— who, as reported a week ago, has been wounded in the ankle and back, after being at the Front only three weeks. A week ago word written in France to his wife ran as follows: "I am in hospital with a slight wound in the ankle from shrapnel. It is the same old ankle that I have always had the bad luck to get hurt. I was wounded at 6 o'clock on Monday morning, and it was mid- night when, I arrived in hospital on Tuesday night. I was also hit in the ribs by a piece of the shrapnel, about one inch long, but my belt saved me from a very severe gash, and the metal has only bruised me; thank God I had my belt on! Well, I daresay there are one or two letters for me up the line, but I don't think I shall ever get them now, because I am 160 miles from where I got hurt. . . I am in very good health, and eating better than I have done for seine time."

On Tuesday morning Mrs. Thomason received a card sent from the Wharncliffe War Hospital, Sheffield: " I arrived here safe at three this morning," it ran. "I hope to be home before very long."—At night another card—which the Private had sent while on the way to England— arrived. '

div.head: Will not Forget the Day-
div.p: Will not Forget the Day-

A letter received yesterday from Privat: Thomason ran: "I myself think I am improv- ing. I have 'been under-X-rays to-day, so I shall soen know now whether they have got all the 'old iron' out. If it is not all out I shall have to go under an operation towards the week-end. can manage to knock about a bit on two sticks; but they Won't let me; I have to lie down all the time. But I guess it is for the best. I shall not forget the day. I got hurt in a hurry, I can tell you. I will tell you all about it when I come home. I shall have seven days' furlough when I got better, and then I expect I shall be bound for Chester with the others. lam wounded in the right ankle and right side ribs, and a few small bits caught me on the left knee. but the hurt to the ankle is the worst.. Fred Kay was the one who helped me up to the dress- ing station. I was in the next hospital to George Taylor at Letreport, but I did not know until I saw it in the paper." Private Thomas-on, who is aged 34, was born at Lymm, being the eldest son of Mrs. Isaac Thomason, of Rush Green. /liter leaving the Oughtrington Schools he entered the employ- ment of Mr. Ingham, butcher, of Heatley ; and later he went to work at the Ship Canal brick- yard; but• previous to the outbreak of war he worked as an assistant at the new go-operative Stores. He- had been for eight years in the Territorials. He is married, and has one child —a little girl. •

div.head: PRIVATE UEOME TAYLOR.
div.p: PRIVATE UEOME TAYLOR.
Soon Leave Beatiitful French Town—
For England.

Mrs. G. Oldham, of Rush Green, received on Thursday night a letter from her son, Private George Taylor—who was hurt in the stomach by slipping on to a bayonet. It was written from the Letreport Canadian Hospital. and stated: "I am improving very nicely so far. I have had a letter from Harry [l4th Cheshires, now in Walesl, and he is all right. I am very sorry to hear about J.-Zones; I hope he will soon reCover from his illness. I don't think it will be long now before they move me—l expect to come to some hospital in England, as, I am doing fine. We do get well looked after here; we get every- thing we want. lam still on the same diet, but I don't mind that, so long as I am improving. It is very lovely where we are, only a few Yards from the sea; and I believe it is a beautiful little town."

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN W. JONES.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN W. JONES.
Visited At London By His Soldier-
Father.

div.head: SUNDAY FIGHTING.
div.p: SUNDAY FIGHTING.
Corporal George Appleton Looks On The Bright Side.
Corporal George Appleton, of the 14th Light Division, 42nd Infantry Brigade—whose home is at Cross Brow, Statham—writes from the Front to a friend

"I am. pleased to say I am going on Al, • although we do have some awful and very trying experiences; but we must hope that they won't last for ever! I heard from home that you had had some soldiers billeted in Lymm, and at the Sunday schools. I wish I could go to Sunday school; in fact, we hardly know when it is Sunday—the fight goes on whatever day it may be. I hope you made all the boys as comfortable as possible—as I judge by your letter that you did—for we were always made welcome wherever we went when in England. When they get out here they will find it a great change. Keep on smiling! We shall all be together again by next year, I hope. . ."

div.head: PRIVATE FRED DANIELS.
div.p: PRIVATE FRED DANIELS.
News Of His Death After Being Shot In Head Confirmed.

Private Frederick Daniels, of the 3rd South Lancashire Regiment—whose home was at West Hyde, Lymm—has given his life at the Front. As we stated last week, the news first came in a letter received by Mr. Starkey, lately of the Brook Inn, Latchford. A comrade of Private Daniels wrote that he saw him fall and lie quite still. The news has now been confirmed in the fol- lowing : " Army Pay Office, Shrewsbury. I regret to state that information has reached this office of the death of 16044 Private F. 'Daniels, of the South Lancashire Regiment.—F. E. Kingsbor- ough, Regimental Paymaster. 27/7/15." Private W. Jinks, a comrade, wrote to a friend: "Fred Daniels got killed 'last Monday (the 12th). He was hit in the head, and didn't suffer. I believe he dropped just like a log, and never moved after." • ( The dead Private leaves a widow and four young children. Prior to his enlistment shortly
after the outbreak of war, Private Daniels was

employed at Long's Tannery, Grappenhall Thirty-eight years of age, he was one of the seven sons of Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Daniels, of Clay-terrace, Booth's Hill. He was born in Lymm, and attended the Parish School.

div.head: PRIVATE T. W. SHEPHEIRD.
div.p: PRIVATE T. W. SHEPHEIRD.
Ills Death Confirmed After A Three
Months' Suspense.

Private Thomas William Shepheard, of the 2nd Cheshires—whose home was with his mother, Mrs. Costello,. at 4, West Hyde, Lymm —is now known, to have given his life .at the Front. ,Recently we published particulars of his case—he had taken part in heavy .fighting two months before, and since May Bth had been missing. Little hope of his survival had been enter- tained, and the fears of his relatives • and friends have now proved not ill-founded; for on Saturday his mother received from the Records ,Office at Shrewsbury a letter which stated that he was killed in action on May Bth, and buried by the Germans- amongst their dead but in his own religion, near Wielge or Ypern. div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Came Home from the Front to Wed.—Miss Selina Webb, third daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Webb and of Mrs. Webb, of 22, Caw- dor-street, Stockton Heath, and late of Tunnel House, Preston Brook, was, at Daresbury Parish Church, last week, married to Quartermaster- Sergeant Harry Kendal, of the Army Remount Department, who is stationed in' France, and who is the eldest son of Mi. and Mrs. Chris- topher Kendal, of Exeter. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Albert Webb, and was attired in a charming dress of cream silk crepe le chene, with a Leghorn hat trimmed with orange blossom and an ostrich plume. She car- ried a dainty bouquet of lilies, white carnations and smilax, and wore a gold and diamond brooch, the gift of Mrs. Andrew, oT Teignmouth. The bridesmaids were the Misses Miriam and May Webb (the sisters of the bride), Miss Nina Kendal (a sister of the bridegroom), and Miss Mabel Webb (a niece of the bride). Each wore a gold ibrooch, with the crest of the bride- groom's regiment on it, these being the gifts of the gallant Quartermaster-Sergeant. Tire two elder bridesmaids wore pale blue satin dresses, with hats to match, and they carried bouquets of pink carnations and smilax. The two younger bridesmaids were dressed in white em- broidered muslin, and wore pale blue sashes. They carried baskets of sweet _peas. Mr. Fred Kendal (the bridegroom's brother) acted as best man, • and Miss Houghton played appropriate selections on the organ. Following the mar- riage ceremony a reception was held at The Up- lands, Moore, kindly lent for the occasion by Miss Andrew. The honeymoon is being spent in North Wales. There were numerous presents.

div.head: GRAPPEN HALL.
div.p: GRAPPEN HALL.

Sunday Scholars' Excursion.—The members of Mrs. Howard's class at the Independent Metho- dist Church had an enjoyable outing to Frod- sham on Thursday. Mrs. Howard has succeeded her late husband as teacher of the class in question.

For Convalescent Soldiers.—The Thelwall Heyes Military Convalescent Home was again thrown open to the public on Thursday, and many availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting the comfortable institution. Visitors were asked to bring gifts of groceries, fruit, &e., and a useful addition to the pantry was the result of the request. Tea was served to the visitors at a moderate charge.

Independent Methodist Sunday School Treat. —The annual treat in connection with the Inde- pendent Methodist Sunday School was held on Saturday in.a field kindly lent by Mr. Bradford. of Reddish Hall. Most of the scholars reached the rendezvous afoot, but the smaller ones were conveyed in lurries. A good tea was served. after which the usual games were indulged in until the fall of dusk signalled the time for the homeward journey. Mr. Henshall (the school superintendent) was in .charge.

div.head: AN ADVERTISEMENT BOARD..
div.p: AN ADVERTISEMENT BOARD..
Ship Canal Co. Obdurate.

The following letter was read at Tuesday's meet- ing of the Runcorn Rural District Council, from the Manchester Ship Canal Co., in a reply to a complaint about the erection of an advertise- ment board near the Swing Bridge at Latch- ford Without

"I have had the matter inquired into, and find that you are mistaken in stating that an advertisement hoarding has been erected. All that has been done is to put up another enamel plate, 4ft. by Bft., and I am informed that this is not at all unsightly. I may mention that the company have had application for the use of the land for other purposes, and, of eoursei must be free to develop the undertaking to the best advantage."

Mr. Mclntyre remarked that the complaint was that the company had had a hoarding erected similar to the one that they at Stock- ton Heath had had abolished, but it appeared it was only a bad imitation of that one. (Laugh- ter.)

Mr. Pilling said that it was erected beside the prettiest house in the neighbourhood. The people living there had been at great pains to get the place right, and it was quite a treat to stop and look at the place. He hoped the Council would see their way to make further objection. The advertisement was quite large enough to be a nuisance. . Mr. Wright seconded, and it was agreed that a turther objection to the advertisement be made to the company.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesleyan Sisterhood.—The closing meeting of the Sisterhood's 1914-15 session was held on Tuesday afternoon, when a paper on "Sankey's hymns" was given by Mrs. W. J. Bate. The paper was interspersed with solos, duets, recita- tions, Sze., by the members, and greatly contri- buted ;to the interest of the meeting. div.head: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
Neutrality In The War Morally Impossible.

At the Wesleyan Conference at Birmingham on Saturday, the draft of the pastoral address to the churches was submitted and approved. It, reviewed the present situation and made a call to the Church to face the duties of the hour. Referring to the war the address said the part Great Britain was, playing in this stupendous conflict was dictated by national honour and not by a selfish expediency. It was morally impossible for the nation to remain neutral while Belgium was ravaged and France and Russia were imperilled, and the gains of Christianity' and civilisation jeopardised by a despotic ambition.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.

NEXT YEAR'S ROYAL AT MANCHESTER. The Duke of Portland, president of the Royal Agricultural Society, at a citizens' meeting held at ,Manchester, .moved a resolution supporting the .action -of the City Council in inviting the society to visit Manchester next year. It was absolutely necessary, he said, that those con- nected with and interested in agriculture should use their skill and do their utmost to produce and conserve the food of the nation. It was impossible to say how long the war would last, but it was likely to be of some duration, and would strain to the utmost the resources of the nation in men, money and the staple articles of food. He believed that the holding of the show would tend to co-ordinate and strengthen the agricultural industry of the country. It was possible that contingencies might arise which would make it essential to reconsider the whole question of holding the show. The resolution was seconded by Lord Shuttle- worth. _
Sir Gilbert Greenall said that a show field had been placed at their disposal by Earl Eger- ton of Tatton.

The resolution was carried and a committee appointed. At the monthly meeting of the Royal Agri- cultural Society held• on Wednesday reports from several committees were presented and adopted with regard to the show, which will he held in the week beginning Monday, June 26. The Council had granted a sum of £6,000 for prizes, and a sub-committee had been ap- pointed to draft.a prize sheet and list of judges It has been decided to hold ''a flower 'show. A special feature will be the offer of prizes for bottled vegetables as well as bottled fruits. and an extended classification for cheese is being arranged. The Chemical Society of London has constituted itself a consultative body to assist the nation by endeavouring to organise and utilise the chemical talent of the country, and at the invitation of that institution the Council had nominated six chemical experts to advise the Chemical Society with regard to all problems, inventions, and suggestions bearing upon agriculture.

div.head: BRITISH CROPS DISCOURAGING.
div.p: BRITISH CROPS DISCOURAGING.

Our special crop reports for July let are cer- tainly discouraging, and it is to be hoped that the later reports will be more favourable. All our crops have suffered, first from a cold, wet and prolonged winter, and later from protracted drought and cold nights. All are under average, and especially those planted in the spring. For the first time we have found it impossible to frame a statement as to the average for swedes and turnips, on account of so manindefinite reports, such as "too early," "'few sown,f, 'not up," or "being resown." Many corre- spondents decline figures, and merely express the above facts in words which, of course, can- not be used for calculating averages. In war time bounteous crops would have been particu- larly welcome, but with the exception of Man- gels, which are notably drought-resisting, all fall below the previous ten years' average.— "The Times."

div.head: IN THE WAR ZONE.
div.p: IN THE WAR ZONE.

A Gordon Territorial officer, with an evident bent for agriculture, gives his impressions of farming within the war zone. "It looks strange," he writes, "'to see a well-sown field with a few 'Jack Johnson' holes in it, or a number of cows in a byre which may gOt . a shell through the wall any day. The soil is very fertile. It was evident that farmers ad- hered to systems of rotation. The most common cereal is rye; barley, wheat and Oats are also grown. We shall have to get a',move on if the crops are to be harvested,' continues the writer. "Two crops which are often seen are tobacco and hops. Many farms have got two or three good horses, also a few cows. The milk is sold to soldiers at a high figure. Sheep are com- paratively rare, but there are 'quite a lot of pigs and poultry. Implements are more antiquated than ours. Carts have two medium-sized wheels in rear and a small one in front." The officer saw the flail used often, but he has not seen a steading with a threshing mill. Dap are used for pulling light carts; they are also used to drive churns and separators by means of a treadmill.—" N.B. Agriculturist."

These are indispensable in even small gardens, and to have a good supply during the winter several sowings should be made during August. div.head: SOUL OF A NATION.
div.p: THE SOUL OF A NATION.
Drumhead Service On St. Paul's Cathedral Steps.
For what is a man profited if he sball,gain the whole world and lose his own soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?— Matthew xvi. 26.

From this text the Bishop of London, on Sunday, standing on the steps of St. Pa.urs Cathedral, delivered to a vaster congregation than. could have assembled within the walls of Wren's great building, an address of inter- cession and a call to prayer and sacrifice. The scene was a memorable one. As far as the eye could reach down Ludgate-hill and along • the Strand the pavements were packed with people whom not even the torrential rains that fell almost throughout the service could drive into shelter. They waited patiently the arrival Of the long procession of soldiers, wh• ,had marched, with the Bishop of London in their midst, from Trafalgar-square, along the Strand and Fleet-street, to St. Paul's Cathedral,. The regiments represented in the march were theist to the Bth Battalions of the City of Lon- don Territorial Regiments and the Honourable Artillery Company, and in addition the let, 2nd and 3rd London Field Ambulance. The band of the H.A.C. headed the procession, followed by the Royal Field Artillery Band. Outside the Cathedral the troops, numbering about 4,000, were formed up in a semi-circle facing the steps. The drums of the H.A.C. formed an altar for the service, and the Bishop delivered his address standing in front of them.
The service opened with the singing of "0 God, our help in ages past," and this was ' followed by the Bishop's address, which he called "The Sçul of a Nation.'

div.head: ENGLAND'S SOUL.
div.p: ENGLAND'S SOUL.

Speaking from the text quoted, Dr. Winning- ton-Ingram recalled "Punch's" famous car, lieprodnced at the time "Ph, Examiner;", in .which a-sinister figure, repra- "aerinsukt, -Says sneeringly to the King of Belgium:- "So you have lost-everything' ;- and King Albert answered back, "Not my soul."
[smiting_
It was, a great answer and a true ore-, the Bishop said; the soul of a nation was more •than its material possessions. Belgium had found her soul, and so, too, had France and Russia.

"The Church," proceeded the Bishop, "has come out to-day to give a message to the soul of our nation. Have we got a soul? Who that knows the history of the English people can doubt it. The children would not be springing from all over the world to the mother's side if the mother had no soul, if, there had been no love for freedom, no belief in honour, no care for the weak, no contempt for the merely strong, there would have been no glad loyalty from thousands and tens of thousands who have rallied round the flag. " Could we admit for a moment that the soul of the nation which won Agincourt, which flung back the Armada, which withstood for so ,many years the armies of Napoleon is not as great as the soul of other nations? Rather we believe that in this contest on the Continent it is the soul of England which is once again to free the world. No calamity can be pictured more awful than if at this supreme crisis in the history of the world England should fail." But, if we were to rise to our vocation, it was essential that, as a nation, not as a few gfoups of pious individuals, we should turn to God. A call had been addressed to the nation by its responsible leaders for "universal volun- tary service." It was the greatest call that could be addressed to a nation, and no other nation but England believed it possible. Every- one knew it was the last time we could afforl to leave the call voluntary, but if it could be given, voluntary service was the noblest kind of service.
—But," Dr. Winnington-Ingram went. on, " there must be something more even than. Bp- vice; we must alSo- save.

"We summon then, the soul of England Up arise in all its grandeur and strength ett this crisis of the day of God. Come from the 'four- winds, thou Breath of the Spirit. and breathe upon this, great people, that hope and faith and love may once again revive and the world be saved again by the 'Soul of a People." Following the Bishep's addrees, the hymn beginning,
0, Lord of life, to Thee we cry
For courage and for, victory,

was sung, and in this, as in the first hymn, great numbers of the people joined fervently. The intercessions were intoned by three of the Cathedral clergy, and the Cathedral choristers led the responses, in which very many of the congregation took part.

div.head: CHAPTER ON PARISH CLERKS.
div.p: A CHAPTER ON PARISH CLERKS.
Church Dignitary Whose Glory Has Long Since Departed.

div.head: WONDERFUL MUSIC OF LONG AGO.
div.p: THE WONDERFUL MUSIC OF LONG AGO.
By ARTHUR

It is true that the Parish Clerk survives. Re receives fees at weddings and funerals, and may be found, if sought, on Sundays near the door or at a bell rope. But the figure of whom we write has vanished, and it demands the skill of the artist, as well as the pen of a rea4y writer, to bring him back. He no longer walks the aisle with stately footfall, and takes his place as leader of the service, in the stall of the three-decker pulpit. Gone the, gown and bands; gone the ecclesiastical ha;t_.and rod of office; gone the voice that said, "Let us sing to the glory of God the Heasthr 'lnt that has Allelnyah at the bend of hevety line,"

The Parish Clerk of whom we would write has gone, save that he lives vividly in the youthful memories of old churchgoers who, with all his failings, would like to have him back, and hear his sonorous "Amen.". But we must begin with facts that lie far, farbeyond the longest memory. For the Clerk is ten ancient institution. Ancient drawings upoa manuscripts preserved in the British Mnastiza reveal him at the dawn of the Church's history assisting the clergy in their Va.thol2B offices. His title " clericus " marks him as having held an honoured office,, and tka official title to this day for a clergyman is that of "clerk in holy orders." He lived thritugh the dark ages and the changes of the Reformation, to be killed at last by the Oxford movement and the removal of the three-decker pulpit, which was his throne. He varies, of course, with the ages. Ch*icer gave us a capital picture of him as "Jolly Absolom," who could sing well, let blood, clip and shave, make a charter for land, danoe with the friskiest maiden and sing lots of.things besides Psalms. A man who could be- at once the village lawyer, barber, physi- dam, clown and priest, was clearly no nonentity, and Chaucer is interesting in his statement that the clerk carried incense and holy water to the homes of the parishioners, reeeving presents for his maintenance in retupa.

gn-ch was the village clerk before the Reformation. After the Reformation he went round for fees, but did not take the cener nor water sprinkler. In pre-Reforma- tiou times there was a verger, reader and ,examist. At the Reformation all these were merged into one, and the Parish Clerkship in- creed mightily in importance therebecause. There was no longer the sprinkling and incetse, for which he could receive fees, but anbetitutes were found. A Holy Loaf was made and blessed, and portions carried round and sold. As perquisites he received from tearishioners a loaf at Christmas, eggs at Easier, and sheaves at harvest. Then there were the " church ales " made from malt that was given to him and sold to all and sundry. Pnritanism banished the " clerke-ales," and the bitter cry went up that the clerks were left without income.

div.head: MEN OF MANY PARTS.
div.p: MEN OF MANY PARTS.

A °lea without an income must have been a sore spectacle and a blot upon Merrie Eng- land, for he performed a perfect string of duties. It was he who opened the church at daybreak, greased and rang the bells, trimmed anti lighted the lamps, strewed the floor with rnahes, cleaned the gutters, 4ecorated for feast days, and, lest the hours dragged, taught the children of the parish. On Sundays he read the Epistle and led the singing, read at funerals, communion and weddings, extracted dogs, kept a controlling eye upon boys, sleepers, the parson, and the deer.

It is of the clerk of a century ago, this man of many parts, that we wish to write. True, the Commonwealth period reduced his status, and the abolition of church rates reduced his income, but he survived with majesty scarce abated until the modern movement relegated hint to the bell rope and the churchyard. To appreciate the Parish Clerk we must re- member that the services were very great things in those days. If the service fell less than two hours in length there was the feeling that a tradition had been violated or that somebody had been deprived of their rights. The ser- mon lasted an hour or more, and psalms were linen out two lines at a time and sung to the droning accompaniment of fiddles and flutes. The only person who was reasonably com- fortable under all these sufferings was the squire, whose pew had a separate stove and protecting curtains. He alone could snore without fear of the "bobber," and had the additional privilege of banging the stove door ass signal that the sermon was getting un- bearable.

A century ago the service could not begin until the squire had marched up the aisle to hill luxurious pew. In one parish the clerk clintlied upon the communion table and stood looking through the window until he caught sight of the squire, climbing down to tell the cletgyman that he might come out and begin. Sometimes it would happen that the squire arrived late, whereupon the minister would stop in his reading, apologise for having begun, and turn back to the beginning. On one occasion the clergyman, without looking into the squire's pew, began the open- ing sentence, "When the wicked man -" Hold on," yelped the clerk, "he hasn't +comb. yet."

div.head: CLERK AS MUSICIAN.
div.p: THE CLERK AS MUSICIAN.

Bat it is of the clerk and not the squire that we are to be reminiscent. In the 91st eantln of the Church of England it is laid clown that the clerk should be distinguished " for his competent skill in singing." It fell to him to announce the psalms and lead in the music. There was no organ to soothe the wages; a pitch-pipe was often the only instru- ment. They sang the psalms in Tate and Brady's version, which were given out in terms something like the following; "Let as sing to the praise and glory of God the one hundred and sevingth psalm, first, second and +sieving and all the other verses with the doxology." If there were a choir it was placed in the west gallery and the clerk would then strut down the aisle, climb the stairs, blow his pipe, and give the basses, tenors and the rest their separate note, which they would hang on to in a humming tone until the clerk had got back to his place in the bottom deck of the pulpit. Then with a wave and a cranb the. music would begin- There was 'usually a muddle about the Doxology, for they were all placed at the 'end of the book and awed section of the congregation or choir was sure to get a Doxology that had two syllablee too few or too many. Many village Churches a century ago had a band. There were fiddles, flutes, bassoons, and often a drum. These made great work of the psalms. and not even the squire could sleep through them. The clerk conducted from his desk, though he often went up to the•gallery to get better control.
When it is remembered that the clerk read nub the lines two at a time, and then got the orchtstra and singers through them, it can be imagined that psalm-time often brought

div.head: MOUNFIELD.
div.p: MOUNFIELD.

embarrassment and temporary difficulty. But the clerk seldom failed to come out at the other end. Canon Gregory Smith says that his clerk, when the fiddles and fifes tangled the music, would stop the noise and say calmly to the congregation, " Beg pardon, gents, wee'l try again."

div.head: CLERKS' ENGLISH.
div.p: CLERKS' ENGLISH.

Very much more troublesome than the music were the words. When the 104th Psalm was to be sung there came that word Leviathan. But clerks were bold and did not quail at trifles. One vicar tells that his clerk who was a cobbler always called it the leather- thing; another read it "the lieutenant whom thou hest made to play therein," and another, "the great live thing." The clerk of Lech- ' hampton so the minister wrote, always read, "I am become a pelican in the wilderness and an owl in the desert," in Psalm cii. 6, as "a pay cock in a wild-doek's nest and a howl in the desert." Another clerk did not know the word "alien," and always said he was "a lion to my mother's children," when reading the lesson. Yet another was troubled by "Awed," and read out the hymn "A -wed by thy presence." A Cornish clerk who was "not much of a scholard," and who knew more about horses than Biblical lore used to read "I have seen the wicked spreading him- self like a great bay horse." The vicar re- monstrated without success.. It was true the book said "Green bay tree," but how could a thing be green and, bay at the same time. The psalmist must have meant a bay horse— a thing everybody understood. There is a chapter in the Book of Daniel that was a sore trial to many clerks. It con- tains the names Shaclrach, Meshach, and Abednego, repeated ten or a dozen times. A South Country vicar says that his clerk would get through the names once and then say afterwards "the gentlemen mentioned " each time he encountered the Hebrew worthies. A Lancashire clerk had the same trouble and got over it the same way, but each time he pushed in the phrase "them three as ah said afore."

div.head: OLD TIMES, OLD MANNERS.
div.p: OLD TIMES, OLD MANNERS.

Many things happened a century ago that are beyond all belief to-day. Archbishop Tait once said that no ode could look back upon the church services of the past without a kind of shame at the memory, and we quote his words lest it should seem that our stories and gleanings are given in malice- . Here is a word picture given by the late Mr. Beresford Hope of church services in a market town in Surrey.. "The aisles were filled with family pews or private boxes, raised aloft, and approached by private doors and staircases. These were owned by the magnates of the place, who were wont to bow their recognitions across the nave. There was a decrepit west gallery for the band, and the ground floor was crammed with crazy pews of every shape. The pulpit stood against a pillar, with reading desk and clerk's box underneath.. The ante-communion ser- vice was read from the desk, separated from the liturgy and sermon by such renderings of Tate and Brady as the unruly gang of volun- teers with fiddles and wind instruments in the gallery pleased to contribute, The clerk, a wizened old fellow in a brown wig, repeated the responses with a nasal twang, and with a substitution of w for v, and after the Nicene Creed this worthy announced meetings at the town inn of the executors of a deceased duke. Two hopeful cubs of the clerk sprawled be- hind him in the desk, and the back-handers occasionally intended to reduce them to order were apt to resound against the impassive boards. During the sermon this zealous ser- vant of the sanctuary would take up a broom and sweep out the middle alley, in order to save himself the fatigue of a weekday visit."

div.head: SOME APPALLING EFFECTS.
div.p: SOME APPALLING EFFECTS.

Of the music that floated from the church gallery, P. H. Ditchfield, a venerable and re- spected clergyman has told us some enter- taining things.. They had remarkable times in those days. In one of them the first part of the line was repeated thrice and gave such results as the following:— Take thy pill; Take thy pill; Take thy pilgrim home.. It also led the male voices into sighing for My own sal; My own sal; My own salvation's rock to praise. " My poor poll; My poor poll"; was the preclude to "My poor polluted heart." Another time repeated the first four sylla- bles in the line in the same way. The young women led ,off Oh, for a man; Oh, for a man; and the men crashed in to explain that they meant "A mansion in the skies." The same time gave: And in the pie; And in the pie; And in the pious he delights-. And also: •
Stir up this stew; Stir up this stew; This stupid heart of mine.
After the day of the bassoon and fiddle came the short and memorable day of the barrel organ, to do justice to which we shall have to ask space for another article.

div.head: DEATH OF JUDGE GURNER
div.p: DEATH OF JUDGE GURNER
A Quiet Funeral.

As we briefly announced last Saturday, his Honour Judge Henry Edward Garner died on Wednesday last week at his London residence, 36, Barkston Gardens, S.W., after an illness of only two days' duration, at the age of 61, to the great sorrow of a very large circle of acquaint- ances by whom he was held in the highest regard for his geniality and kindly nature and unostentatious disposition.

The late Judge was the younger son of the late Mr. Henry Field Gurner, upwards of 40 years Crown Solicitor of Melbourne, Australia. He was ea-u'eated privately at Cheltenham and Cambridge Trinity College. He married in. 1890 Eva Isabel, younger daughter of the late Mr: John Barter Bennett, of Melbourne and London, and has one daughter and one son, Gerard—who is at Eton. He was a very old popular member of the Garrick Club. He was appointed Judge to Circuit 7 (which incl Salford, Warrington, Leigh, Runcorn, Alt_ ham and Birkenhead) a year back—as from 'July, 1914—but he had previously sat as deputy for County Court judges; and therefore came equipped with a large knowledge of, and ex- perience in the work. div.head: COUNTY COURT REFERENCES.
div.p: COUNTY COURT REFERENCES.
At the sitting of the Warrington County Court on Thursday. reference was made to the decease of his honour Judge .Gurner, which occurred last week.

Mr. Sellars, deputy-judge, said that when he presided at the Court on the previous Thurs- day he did so in the belief that he was acting during the illness of Judge Gurner, and little thought that Judge Gurner had passed away. He regretted to say that the late Judge was suddenly taken ill on the Monday and passed away on Wednesday afternoon. It seemed to him thai, before they commenced business that morning they should pay a tribute of respect to the memory of the late Judge. Although, per- sonally, he had not had the privilege of know- ing Judge Gurner, he had heard on all sides that lie was a judge of great impartiality, of great justice and of very determined character.

div.head: TRIBUTE OF THE BAR.
div.p: THE TRIBUTE OF THE BAR.

Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the solicitors practising at the Court, associated himself with the remarks of the Judge. The late Judge Gurner's death was terribly sudden, and they were absolutely ignorant last Thursday that he had passed away. There had been many changes during the last few years in that Court, but who had thought they were so soon to have a further one. He, personally, much regretted Judge Gurner's death. Mr. T. J. Ridgway (registrar) concurred. He said that his Honour had told him he was not well, that he had been ordered to take a rest, and that his doctor had suggested that he ought not to complete the sessions, finishing on Thurs- day. But Judge Gurner's strong sense of duty impelled him to go on with his work till the beginning of the vacation. He (Mr. Ridgway) spoke on behalf of himself and his staff when he expressed deep regret at the loss of Judge Gurner.

div.head: NEW COUNTY COURT JUDGE.
div.p: NEW COUNTY COURT JUDGE.
Sheffield Recorder To Succeed
Judge Gurner.
Mr. John Scott Fox, K.C., who has been Recorder of Sheffield for nearly a dozen years, has been appointed County Court Judge for this circuit in succession to the late Judge H. E. Gurner.

Mr. Scott Fox, who took his seat as Recorder at Sheffield Quarter Sessions for the first time in January, 1904, was born at Selby on the 17th January, 1852, and he is therefore in his 64th year. He is the son of the Rev. William Fox. He was educated at Bedford Grammar School, afterwards proceedins to Oxford University. In 1877 he obtained his M.A., and 8.C.L., and be- came a barrister, joining the North-Eastern Circuit in 1881. From 1884 to 1891 he was Examiner to the Court; he filled the position of Revising Barrister from 1885 to 1896, and was made Queen's Counsel in 1898. He was Solicitor- General to the County Palatine Durham in 1901, and three years later was appointed Recorder of Sheffield, in succession to the late Mr. Stuart Macaskie.

He has always been a hard worker, and built up an excellent practice; as a pleader he proved himself both alert and painstaking, and the same qualities', coupled with a strict fairness, have marked his judicial career. May Remain Recorder.

It will be a source of satisfaction to members of the Bar practising in Sheffield and his numerous other friends in the city and district, says the "Sheffield Telegraph," that Mr. Scott Fox's new appointment will not neces- sarily involve his retirement from the position of Recorder. There are several precedents for the hol4ing of the dual offices. Indeed, the neigh- bouring county of Lincoln furnishes an ex- ample, for his Honour Sir George Sheraton- Baker, who is County Court Judge for this cir- cuit, also holds the position of Recorder of Barnstaple- and Bideford, ,in Devonshire,

div.p: PRIVATE JOHN CARTWRIGHT.
Still Bedfast In An East Anglian
Hospital.

Private John Cartwright, of the 2nd •South Lancashires, who was wounded in the foot, has written to his mother, who resides at 27, Dixon- street, to say that he is still in the Lakenham Military Hospital, Norwich, and that he is going on as well as can be expected, although he is still bedfast, as his injured foot is in splints. Discovered To Be A Prisoner In Germany,

Private William A. Thomas, of the 48th Highlanders (Canadian Regiment) who was re- ported missing as far back as April 21st, has been discovered to be a prisoner of war in the hands of the Germans. He is interned at Cattick, in Hunland, and is suffering from gas poisoning.

div.head: FOUR SOLDIER BROTHERS.
div.p: FOUR SOLDIER BROTHERS.
Proud Father Receives Letter Of Thanks From The King.

Mr. E. Fellows, of 295, Liverpool-road, War- rington, has four sons serving in JIM. Forces. This fact was brought to the notice of the King, with the reeult that the proud father of so patriotic a quartet has received the following letter, signed by the Keeper of the Privy Purse, and written from Buckingham Palace:—

Sir,—l am commanded by the King .to convey to you an expression of his Majesty's appreciation of the patriotic spirit which has prompted your four sons to give their services, at the present time, to the Army. The. King was much gratified to hear of the manner in which they have so readily responded to the call of their Sovereign and their country, and I am to express to you and to them his Majesty's congratulations on having contributed in so full a measure to the great cause for which all the people of the British Empire are so bravely fight- ing.

div.p: All In Different Regiments.

div.head: Where They Worked.
div.p: Where They Worked.

At the outbreak of the war Sydney and Tom were employed by Messrs. Dolan and Son, builders and contractors, and before that they worked for Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd. Arthur was employed in the tube department at Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s works, and Robert worked for Messrs. Peel and Connor, of the Adelphi Works, Salford, being a tele- p.itone inspector. div.p: Father An Old "Non-Corn."

div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
A TIP-TOP BILL AT THE 'DROME.

Business at the Hippodrome just as it has been for several weeks past—is this week of the order which is generally described as "bumper." the place being filled to overflow- ing twice nightly. And the pyogramme is of that degree of excellence which warrants such excellent support on the part of a discerning amusement loving public, for there is not a single weak turn in it; the whole " bill" maintaining that high standard of excellence which has established the Macnaghten houses in the upper circles of the vaudeville world. The dominant note in this week's programme is humour; nearly every turn is of a descrip- tion calculated to appeal to the risible faculties. Phil Rees and his Little Coppers present a screamingly funny divertisement—a purely farcical and inoffensive skit on the Police Court Phil, who enacts the part of the Stipendiary, is assisted by an assortment of bright youths who, after enacting the roles of delinquents, are metamorphosed into police- men and proceeded to sing in chorus and dance in step, to the evident delight of patrons in all parts of the house. Will Van Allen, described as "the tramp comedian" with some music added, is original in nearly all that he says and does, and when he is not cracking rich jokes with or at the expense of his audience, he is enchanting their ears with classical selections played with a masterly hand on the tunesome , viola. div.head: ROYAL COURT RE-OPENS.
div.p: ROYAL COURT RE-OPENS.
Recent-breaking Musical Comedy For Holiday Week.

The Royal Court Theatre, Warrington's com- fortable drama-house, re-opens after a short summer interregnum—during which the decorator and the cleaner have been at work— on Bank Holiday. A splendid re-opening at-

traction has been secured, in the shape of "A Chinese Honeymoon," which is a record- breaker among musical comedies, having been played no less than 1,200 consecutive nights at ens West End Theatre—the Strand. The piece .has been judiciously compressed so as to get it into a two-shows-a-night compass, but all the best features in the sprightly dialogue and the tuneful music will be found to have been retained. The piece will be presented by a tip-top company, headed by Miss Itachael Lowe, as Fi-Fi, the whimsical hotel waitress. Miss Lowe is an actress with a big reputation in several branches of theatrical work, and she has been acclaimed by the Press, up and down the country, as a worthy successor to Miss Louie Freear, the famous creator of the part. The cast has been carefully selected and their efforts will be ably supported by a large chorus and an augmented orchestra- Those who have never seen this favourite musical comedy should not miss this opportunity, and those who have seen it before are bound to want to see it again, so that on the whole it is doubtful whether a more popular holiday week booking could have been made.

Nearly twenty years had he served in the Royal Fusiliers, and for seventeen years of that period he had been stationed in India, liurmah and China. Having been recalled

from Calcutta after the outbreak of war, he for some time acted as an instructor in Kite-hener's Army, until he was summoned to rejoin his regiment, with whom he proceeded to the Dardanelles. Killed in the Gulley of Death. At the latter place he took part in several engagements, including the famous charge through the Gully Ravine, which has been dubbed "the Gully of Death," and it was there that he met his fate, being killed instantly. Sergeant-Major Rustage was a Warrington man, and was well known and highly respected. SAPPER JAS. LOCKHART. Fell After Being Out At The Front Twelve Days. After twelve days in France, Sapper James Lockhart, whose home is at 30, Walton-reed, Stockton Heath, has fallen on the field. Sapper Lockhart's wife received the follow- ing letter on Tuesday morning:— "24/7115- " I very much regret to inform you that your husband was killed by shell at 2.30 p.m. to-day. Free Church Out-door Meeting. An open-air meeting in connection with the local Free Church Council was held on Sunday evening, as arranged by Mr. Wm. Beswick. The chair was taken by Mr. Parkes, of the Primi- tive Methodists, who emphasised the need of the magnetising influence of Christ in these times.—The speaker was Mr. Griffiths, of Friars' Green Independent Methodist Church. He declared that the old gospel of the Cross would -never lose its force and weight and value so long as there were men with sins who needed forgiving, who were seeking peace for all their troubles and hope for a brighter and a fuller, life beyond the grave. The early fish gets the hook. David Belasco was condemning two melo- dramas that had had an unmerited success among the less cultivated portion of the public. "The first," said Mr. Belasco, in his epigrammatic way, "was all blood and thunder, and the other was all thud and blunder."
